The widget below lets you feel these costs. It shows a small room with panels at 0.45, 1, 2 and 4 m, and buttons of different sizes. Pick a technique and run a block of trials: hit the highlighted button as fast as you can. The widget adds simulated noise, which it states on screen, and plots time and errors per target, with a running estimate of throughput and of arm effort.

Selection lab. Choose a technique, press Start, and hit the orange target button. With a mouse, aim by moving and confirm by clicking; on a touch screen, put your finger down to aim, slide, and lift to confirm. Simulated: hand-ray jitter of 0.35° that grows with distance in centimetres, plus a 0.6° kick at the confirm (Heisenberg effect); eye-tracking error of about 1°; dwell selection after 450 ms on any button (Midas touch); direct touch only within 0.65 m, with 1 cm fingertip noise and an occasional depth misjudgment, and a simulated step toward far panels. Arm effort uses the shoulder-torque model and Rohmert’s endurance curve of section 4.1 (toy parameters). Small, far targets defeat gaze; depth and reach defeat touch; rays tire the arm.

3. Spatial UI structure

3.1 Windows, volumes and immersive spaces

Every current platform organizes content into three kinds of container. On visionOS (HIG: Designing for visionOS), apps start in the Shared Space, “where multiple apps can run side-by-side and people can open, close, and relocate windows”. Windows are glass planes with a window bar and resize controls; volumes hold 3D content that can be viewed from any angle; an ImmersiveSpace is unbounded, “the system allows only one immersive space to be open at a time”, and opening one hides all other apps (a Full Space). Android XR (design guidelines) has a Home Space for multitasking, in which apps are flat panels (default 1024 × 720 dp), and a Full Space where one app can use spatial panels, orbiters (floating controls attached to a panel) and 3D models. Meta Horizon OS (design guidelines) uses panels and system windows with a control bar and resize handles. HoloLens uses holograms, hand menus, and tag-along or billboarded panels (Microsoft Mixed Reality design docs).

Compared with a phone, this adds two layers of state the user must manage: where each window is in the room, and which mode the system is in (shared or exclusive). A phone has one foreground app on one screen.

3.2 Reference frames: world-, body- and head-locked content

Where content stays when the user moves is decided by its reference frame. Feiner et al. (UIST 1993) already distinguished windows fixed to the head, to the surroundings (the body) and to world objects. The modern vocabulary:

  • World-locked: anchored to a place in the room, like a picture on a wall. Stable, findable by memory, but out of view when you turn away.
  • Body-locked: follows the torso, so it stays around you as you turn your head.
  • Head-locked: follows the head, always at the same spot in view. All platforms advise against it: Apple says it makes people feel “stuck” and breaks Pointer Control and Zoom; Meta says to avoid head-locking HUD content; Microsoft recommends body-locked HUDs instead.
  • Tag-along: a lazy follower that stays put while it is in view and catches up when it would leave the view, keeping content “a glance away” (Microsoft).

Which frame is best depends on the task and the person. Billinghurst et al. (VRAIS 1998) found body-stabilized displays better than head-stabilized ones for search. The Personal Cockpit of Ens et al. (CHI 2014), a body-centric layout of windows, made application switching 40% faster than view-fixed baselines. Belo et al. (arXiv 2608.28064, accepted to IEEE ISMAR 2026) found that users shift from world-anchored to body-anchored UIs while walking, and that no single body anchor wins. For an agent, the lesson is that “place this window” is not one action but a choice of frame, distance and angle, and that the right choice is personal.

3.3 What the guidelines say in numbers

The platform guidelines are unusually quantitative. They define comfort envelopes that are, in effect, constraints for any layout, whether a person or an agent produces it:

3.4 Placement, occlusion, off-view content and multitasking

The guidelines also show what they leave to the user. On visionOS the system places only the first window; after that, people place, resize and arrange windows themselves with gaze + pinch on the window bar and corners. Apple notes that “the system doesn’t provide information about a person’s field of view” to apps. Content can be behind the user, hidden behind another window, or occluded by a real object, and the user has to find it by turning around or recentring. There are 50 classified techniques for occlusion management in 3D visualization (Elmqvist and Tsigas, TVCG 2008), but on a headset most of them are left to the user’s own head and hands.

Multitasking in 3D costs time and comfort. With virtual monitors on a headset, Pavanatto et al. (Frontiers in VR 2023) measured 9.10% slower task completion than a physical workstation (not significant), 37% lower ratings than a laptop on “could continue comfortably for an hour”, and 24% lower ratings on focus than the workstation. Working in VR for five 8-hour days (Biener et al., TVCG 2022) gave significantly worse ratings on most measures, and 2 of 16 participants dropped out on the first day. Long-term Vision Pro users interviewed by Biener et al. (arXiv 2509.05067) named workflow integration and limited ability to adapt and customize. Window management is the clearest example of spatial work that the platform hands to the user and that research systems already automate (section 7.2).

4. Measured difficulty

4.1 Arm fatigue and “gorilla arm”

Mid-air input tires the arm. Designers called this the gorilla-arm effect long before anyone could measure it. Consumed Endurance (CE) by Hincapié-Ramos et al. (CHI 2014) made it measurable from a skeleton stream. CE models the arm as a lever. It sums the gravitational torques of the upper arm and the forearm-plus-hand about the shoulder,

\[\tau = g\,\big(m\_1 r\_1 + m\_2 r\_2\big), \qquad f = 100\,\frac{\tau}{\tau\_{\max}},\]

where $m_i$ are segment masses, $r_i$ the horizontal distances of their centres of mass from the shoulder, and $f$ the required force in percent of the maximum. Rohmert’s endurance curve then predicts how long that force could be held,

\[E(f) = \frac{1236.5}{(f - 15)^{0.618}} - 72.5 \ \text{s} \quad (f > 15), \qquad \mathrm{CE} = 100\,\frac{T\_{\text{interaction}}}{E(f)}\ \%.\]

The curve gives 385 s at 20% and 7 s at 100% of maximum force. It is asymptotic at 15%: below that, the predicted endurance is unlimited.

The numbers from the paper (wall display, Kinect, standing users):

  • CE correlated with perceived exertion on the Borg CR10 scale with $R^2 = 0.716$ (768 measurements, 16 participants).
  • Across plane positions and arm extensions, CE was lowest for the centre plane (27.23%) and the bent arm (23.44%), with the lowest cell at 15.55% (centre plane, bent elbow). Completion time (about 45 s) and landing error did not differ. In the authors’ words, “differences in fatigue emerge even when other measurements are flat”. A system judged only by time and errors would miss the cost.
  • A mid-air dwell keyboard reached only 4.55 wpm in the best block, with required strength between 9.2% and 20.46% of maximum across the keyboard grid.

The model has known limits. Li et al. (VRST 2023) found that CE overestimates endurance for low-exertion poses and misses extra exertion above 90° of shoulder elevation. The improved model NICER (Li et al., ACM TOG 2024) adds a shoulder-specific endurance function, an empirical term for above-shoulder work, and recovery during rest; its correlation with Borg CR10 was 0.978 and 0.976 for two interaction methods, while CE made no prediction at all in that low-exertion task because of the 15% asymptote. Jang et al. (CHI 2017) modelled how fatigue accumulates over a session.

What this means on current headsets: Luong et al. found that bare hands put the hand 14.3% higher and 66.2% further forward than controllers during ray selection, with more exertion. Apple’s guidelines say direct gestures are “best for infrequent use” and that indirect gestures should be preferred for buttons and common components (HIG: Gestures). Gaze + pinch with the hand resting in the lap sidesteps most of the torque. Fatigue matters most for direct touch, rays, and long sequences such as arranging windows or filling in a form.

4.2 Selection errors

The numbers from section 2 add up to a simple fact: on current headsets, selection misses often. In the car study, 8.8 to 23.5% of selections failed at standstill and 20.4 to 36.0% while driving. Ray selection at 8 m failed 15% (controller) to 33% (hand) of the time, mostly because of the confirm action. On a phone, by comparison, touch typing by 37,370 people had 2.3% uncorrected errors (Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019); misses on large touch buttons are rare enough that nobody reports them.

4.3 Text entry

Text is where the gap to the phone is largest and best measured.

  • Phones: 36.2 wpm on average, with 2.3% uncorrected errors (37,370 volunteers, Palin et al.).
  • Selection keyboards in VR (Speicher et al., CHI 2018, HTC Vive, N = 24): controller pointing was fastest at 15.44 wpm (0.97% errors), then controller tapping 12.69, head pointing 10.20, freehand 9.77 (7.57% errors), continuous cursor 8.35 and the d-pad cursor 5.31 wpm. The fastest built-in method is 43% of phone speed.
  • Head-based typing (Yu et al., CHI 2017): 10.59 wpm with dwell, 15.58 with tap, 19.04 with gesture, and 24.73 after 60 minutes of training.
  • A physical keyboard in VR (Grubert et al., IEEE VR 2018): 41.4 wpm outside VR fell to 26.3 inside; a touchscreen keyboard fell from 23.98 to 11.6. Typing without a view of reality gave 30.86% total errors against 4.64% in reality (McGill et al., CHI 2015). Inexperienced typists lost most: 31.8 against 45.4 wpm, while experienced typists lost little (61.8 against 67.2) (Knierim et al., CHI 2018).
  • Decoding helps: an AR mid-air keyboard with a statistical decoder reached 17.75 wpm with under 1% character errors (Dudley et al., TOCHI 2018). With ideal tracking and simulated auto-correction, the upper bounds were 55.6 wpm with two fingers on a surface and 34.5 wpm with ten fingers in mid-air (Dudley et al., ISMAR 2019).
  • The field as a whole: a database of 176 XR text-entry techniques (Bhatia et al., CHI 2025) reports a mean of 20.36 wpm over 137 techniques with a speed figure (range 2.8 to 55.6), and only 20% of their user studies were longitudinal.

Today’s product keyboards add prediction and swipe, so these lab numbers are lower bounds for current products. But the shape of the result is robust: entering a search query, a URL or a message on a headset takes two to three times as long as on a phone, and the intent behind it is easy to say in words. That makes text entry the most obvious operation to hand to an agent (or at least to dictation plus a model that cleans up the result).

4.4 Learnability and discoverability

The most important difficulty for everyday adoption may be the least studied: not knowing what to do. Khurana et al. (IMWUT 2023) observed 25 novices using four consumer AR applications. “Users struggled to discover the correct gestures, with the majority of errors occurring when participants could not determine the correct sequence of actions to perform or could not evaluate their actions.” In Norman’s terms, these are the gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation, not motor failures. The textbook warns about the same thing for “invisible” voice and gesture commands and lists “design for discoverability” among its system-control guidelines.

Other evidence points the same way. In the review corpus of Dehghani et al. (2021), the ease-of-use theme was illustrated by an owner who wrote that “trying to remember where the buttons are is not instinctual yet”. In the YouTube ethnography of Tran et al. (CHI 2025), some Vision Pro users did not know that Travel Mode existed and had to find out how to enable it. In a Counterpoint test with 10 users, Vision Pro had “a bit of a learning curve when using the eyes, hands and gestures”. And learning is barely measured: only 20% of XR text-entry studies were longitudinal (Bhatia et al.), and Khurana’s study is a single session. Nobody knows whether novice difficulty lasts hours or weeks.

4.5 Cybersickness

Sickness is not caused by the interface logic, but interaction design affects it, and it caps how long anyone can operate a headset. The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) of Kennedy et al. (1993) is the standard measure. The meta-analysis of Saredakis et al. (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2020) pooled 55 articles with 3,016 participants:

  • pooled total SSQ 28.00 (95% CI 24.66 to 31.35), above the “problem” cut-off of 20 borrowed from flight simulators;
  • gaming content highest at 34.26, scenic content lowest at 17.33;
  • a mean of 15.6% of participants dropped out because of sickness, across 46 experiments (possibly inflated, since 22 studies did not report dropouts);
  • no relation with the share of female participants ($r = -0.172$). A review of 71 papers by MacArthur et al. (CHI 2021) found the claimed gender gap confounded by study design.

For agents this cuts both ways. An agent that finishes tasks faster and removes head and view motion shortens exposure. An agent that moves the user’s viewpoint automatically creates passive motion, which is one of the factors that shape sickness, so automated navigation could make sickness worse.

4.6 Cognitive load

The evidence on cognitive load is mixed. A review of 58 studies of AR in learning (Buchner et al., JCAL 2022) concludes that AR seems less demanding than other media, but also that AR glasses can add unnecessary load, and that spatial AR (projection) beats see-through AR. The long-session studies of section 3.4 point the same way. A guiding agent must keep its own overlays lean, because help is one more thing to look at.

4.7 Social acceptability

Some costs are social. Location and audience change people’s willingness to perform gestures in public (Rico and Brewster, CHI 2010). VR glasses are judged acceptable in bed, on a metro or a train, but significantly less so in a living room or a café, where interaction with others is expected (Schwind et al., MobileHCI 2018 Adjunct). Bystanders of camera glasses want to be asked before being recorded (Denning et al., CHI 2014), and in a survey of 1,037 Australians, people who did not own Ray-Ban Stories saw more privacy issues (Kaviani et al., PLOS ONE 2024). And a review of 69 papers found no established methods to measure social acceptability at all (Koelle et al., CHI 2020). Voice, the obvious channel to an agent, carries this cost too.

4.8 Difficulty at a glance

Dimension Phone Headset (measured) Sources
Text entry 36.2 wpm, 2.3% uncorrected errors 5.3 to 15.4 wpm (selection keyboards); field mean 20.4 wpm Palin 2019; Speicher 2018; Bhatia 2025
Selection errors rare on large targets 8.8 to 23.5% (parked car), 20.4 to 36.0% (driving); 15 to 33% for rays at 8 m Sasalovici 2025; Qiu 2026

5. Adoption: does complexity keep headsets out of everyday life?

5.1 The numbers

All unit figures below are analyst estimates unless marked as company-reported; “derived” marks numbers we computed from a published growth rate.

  • Headsets shrank. IDC estimates that AR/VR headset shipments peaked at 11.2 M in 2021, fell to 8.8 M in 2022 (−20.9%) and fell another 23.5% in 2023 (about 6.7 M, derived), then grew 10% in 2024 (about 7.4 M, derived), with Meta at 74.6% share (IDC, 2025-03-25). Counterpoint estimates that VR headset shipments fell 28% in 2025 (Counterpoint, Q4 2025). Omdia estimated that headsets in active use fell 8% to 21.9 M in 2024 and that VR “will remain a niche market as long as it remains in its current form” (Omdia, 2024-12-12).
  • Glasses grew. IDC reports that the XR market including glasses grew 44.4% in 2025, while Meta’s Quest shipments fell 42.3% and display-less glasses became the majority of XR shipments (IDC, 2026-03-23). EssilorLuxottica sold more than 7 M Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta AI glasses in 2025 (company results as reported by UploadVR). These glasses have almost no spatial GUI: voice, a camera and audio.
  • Phones are two orders of magnitude bigger. 1,260.3 M smartphones were shipped in 2025 (IDC, 2026-01-13). IDC’s December 2025 forecast of 14.5 M XR devices for 2025 is about 1.2% of that.
  • The leading vendor is losing money. Meta’s Reality Labs reported USD 2,207 M revenue and an operating loss of USD 19,193 M in 2025 (Meta, 2026-01-28), and USD 443 M revenue with a USD 4,129 M loss in Q3 2026 (10-Q).
  • Forecasts kept missing. In December 2023, IDC expected 8.1 M units for 2023 and 28.6 M for 2027.

5.2 Why people do not buy, and why they stop

  • Price dominates purchase decisions. Among US adults not buying a Vision Pro in February 2024 (Variety VIP+ with CivicScience, N = 1,069; data), 65.5% named price; 22.3% said they were not aware of its capabilities; 20.9% said a phone, TV or laptop suffices; 15% said it is uncomfortable; 13.5% named nausea; 12.2% not enough content; 10.2% isolation.
  • Discomfort and health risk drive discontinuance. Dehghani et al. coded 3,205 Amazon reviews of 10 VR devices (2016 to 2019 generation). Perceived discomfort was 39% of codes, health risk 30%, missing content 21%, external compatibility 21%, and ease of use (“effort expectancy”) 7%. In their survey of 119 users, discomfort lowered continuance intention ($\beta = -0.159$) and usage ($\beta = -0.262$), and health risk lowered continuance ($\beta = -0.234$). Ease of use was not among the measured predictors.
  • Use stays narrow. In spring 2023, 29% of US teens owned a VR device, but only 4% of owners used it daily and 14% weekly (Piper Sandler via CNBC). In 112 YouTube videos of sustained use (about 27 h, mostly Vision Pro), use was mainly media and games; productivity was limited by hardware and apps (Tran et al.).
  • Trying is not buying. After an extensive metaverse trial, almost 100 participants wanted to use headsets more but to buy them less (Hennig-Thurau et al., J. Interactive Marketing 2025), which points to value and price rather than an inability to operate the device.

5.3 Where interface complexity appears

Usability does appear in this evidence, in five forms:

  1. A minor but real theme in owner reviews: 7% of codes, about remembering controller mappings (Dehghani et al.).
  2. A learning curve with eyes, hands and gestures noted by analysts (Counterpoint, 10 testers, not peer-reviewed).
  3. Everyday friction in the interaction layer: no precise input like a mouse, hand tracking failing in the dark, a hidden Travel Mode, window management, missing continuity with phone and PC (Tran et al.).
  4. “Ease of use” and “cognitive affordance” as significant antecedents in acceptance models (Rauschnabel and Ro 2016; Jo and Park 2023), alongside usefulness, comfort and social norms.
  5. “Not aware of its capabilities” (22.3%), a discoverability problem, which is closer to the agent thesis than raw complexity.

There is counter-evidence. Early adopters describe the Vision Pro interface as intuitive (Tafesse, SAGE Open 2026). The fastest-growing device class has almost no GUI at all, which can be read as “simpler interaction wins” (supporting the column) or as “cheaper, lighter and fashionable wins” (not supporting it); the data cannot separate the two, because price, weight and interface simplicity change together. And no survey we found even offers “too hard to use” as an answer.

The honest verdict. Operating 3D interfaces is measurably harder than operating a phone, and this adds to the price, comfort, content and sickness barriers that dominate the adoption evidence. It shows up mainly as learning, discoverability, input precision and configuration effort. An agent can lower these costs. It cannot fix weight, price or sickness. The missing evidence is itself a research opportunity: a longitudinal study of why owners stop using Quest-era and Vision Pro-era devices, with “too hard to use” as an option, does not exist.

6. Accessibility: who is excluded today

XR adds barriers for people whom phones already serve reasonably well. The reviews of Dudley et al. (Virtual Reality 2023) and Creed et al. (UAIS 2023) map them across physical, cognitive, visual and auditory impairments. Gerling and Spiel (CHI 2021) argue that VR assumes a “corporeal standard”, a non-disabled body that stands, turns and raises two hands.

  • Blind and low-vision users. Low-vision participants struggled with details at a distance, depth, and searching for targets. With SeeingVR’s 14 tools (Zhao et al., CHI 2019), all 11 participants completed a menu task that only 4 could complete without aids; visual search fell from 7.51 to 3.98 s. Blind users are excluded from most apps. VRSight (Killough et al., UIST 2025) describes unmodified VR apps from the headset video (a detector trained on 17,691 VR images, depth, OCR and GPT-4o, about 2.3 to 2.6 s per query). Its 9 blind and low-vision participants all found the menu in Rec Room, but only one found the specific button: menu trials had an 11% completion rate. Describing a scene is far easier than operating a 3D UI. Participants asked for d-pad navigation, snapping and row/column reading, in other words for a discrete action space.
  • People with limited mobility. Interviews with 16 people found seven physical-access barriers, from first setup to keeping controllers in view of the headset’s cameras (Mott et al., ASSETS 2020). Seated users cannot easily turn to content behind them; point-of-interest techniques that turn the virtual camera instead of the body help (Franz et al., ASSETS 2021).
  • Older adults. 36 adults aged 60+ using Quest 2 social VR complained about headset weight, eyeglass fit, controllers needing finger dexterity, and too little training (Kalantari et al., Innovation in Aging 2023).
  • Deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Work focuses on captions placed in 3D (Jain et al., DIS 2018) and visual or haptic substitutes for sound (Jain et al., ICMI 2021), not on operating UIs.

The platform accessibility services are the closest thing to an agent layer on headsets today. They read a UI tree and act on behalf of the user:

Platform Services (official names) Can operate Cannot (as documented)
Vision Pro VoiceOver (pinch gestures; look-to-explore; “Describe passthrough”; “Label item”), Zoom, Pointer Control (eyes, head, wrist or finger), Dwell Control, Switch Control, Voice Control system UI, SwiftUI windows, and 3D entities that expose an AccessibilityComponent unlabelled 3D entities; Dwell Control documents tap and scroll only
Android XR TalkBack (pinch gestures, explore mode with a hand pointer, can be turned on by asking Gemini), magnification, hover actions with gaze Android views in panels, through the Android accessibility tree how immersive environments and 3D content are read is not documented
Meta Quest screen reader (under “Settings > Experimental”), color correction, live captions system UI and 2D panel apps with content descriptions immersive apps, which draw their own UI; the checklist items are recommendations
HoloLens 2 voice (“select”, “What can I say?”), eye-gaze Start gesture system shell, Start menu, 2D windows no HoloLens-specific screen reader page found

Sources: Apple Vision Pro User Guide, Android XR help, Meta’s accessibility checklist, HoloLens 2 basic usage. These services enumerate labelled elements and move focus in a reading order. They cannot give spatial structure (what is left, behind, near), cannot act on unlabelled 3D content (most content inside immersive apps), and cannot map a free-form 3D manipulation to a command. The W3C’s XR Accessibility User Requirements ask that all of the interface be reachable with one input method and that no action require several simultaneous inputs; they also name the missing piece, “a need for accessibility API’s that map custom user interface actions to control types”. Those requirements are also the preconditions for a 3D GUI agent.

7. What exists to help, and its limits

7.1 Tutorials and onboarding

Learning to interact is a separate, costly phase of VR use. Chauvergne et al. (CHI 2023) built a framework for VR onboarding from 21 ergonomic reviews of tutorials and 15 expert interviews. Kao et al. (CHI PLAY 2021) analysed 50 popular VR games: 90% had a tutorial level, 88% used text help, 56% diagrams and only 22% labelled the virtual controllers. In four online experiments with 433 headset owners, tooltips attached to the virtual controllers improved learnability in a shooter and a puzzle game but made no difference in a wave shooter and a rhythm game. Help that is anchored in space can work, but tutorials are one-shot, mostly text, and not available later when a user forgets.

7.2 Adaptive and intelligent UIs

A line of research lets the system decide what to show, where and how much, and it already takes over part of the spatial work with measured gains:

System What it does Result
Lindlbauer et al., UIST 2019 rule-based + combinatorial optimization of which apps appear, at what detail, where, from cognitive load −36% secondary-task interactions
SemanticAdapt, UIST 2021 a linear program placing UI by semantic links to physical objects (recipe next to the stove) −33% manual adaptations
AUIT, UIST 2022 toolkit of adaptation objectives (reachability, visibility, consistency) with a real-time solver a reusable objective library
SituationAdapt, UIST 2024 GPT-4V rates where UI may cover the real scene; an optimizer places it ranked first by all 12 participants
DuoZone, arXiv 2511.15676 GPT-4.1 recommends apps and layouts on Vision Pro; users refine by direct manipulation 34.5% faster layout matching; 168 s vs 218 s to build a workspace; NASA-TLX 33 vs 48; 82.8% of layouts accepted
Put-that-there via LLMs, arXiv 2511.02378 GPT-4 fuses a 3D scene, speech, pointing and head gaze into JSON place / remove actions action schema, no user study yet
ConverseMR, arXiv 2610.24640 spoken requests mapped to adaptation objectives speech and direct manipulation are complementary

These systems arrange the UI. None of them operates the content inside the windows, and most run inside their own app, not on the system’s windows. Users accept most but not all proposals (about 17% of DuoZone’s layout suggestions were rejected), and they keep refining spoken commands after seeing the result. And rearranging too often is itself a cost, which is why SemanticAdapt has a consistency term.

7.3 Assistants and voice control on shipping devices

As of November 2026:

Device Assistant Can operate Not documented
Vision Pro (visionOS 27, beta) Siri AI with Visual Intelligence: onscreen awareness, gaze-to-invoke (Apple, 2026-06-08) app actions (messages, playlists, alarms), Environments, accessibility toggles pressing arbitrary buttons or changing arbitrary settings
Vision Pro Voice Control (support page) any named or numbered element: “Tap 3”, “Swipe up at 5”, grid overlays planning: the user names every step
Quest 3 / 3S Meta AI (Meta, 2024-07-23), replacing Voice Commands, to “control your headset hands-free”; vision of the physical room system commands, answers recognition of virtual objects and app UIs
Galaxy XR (Android XR) Gemini (Google): “take action on your behalf across your apps”; “Hey Google, organize these windows” window layout, Maps, YouTube search a list of supported actions; acting inside immersive third-party apps

Gemini’s “organize these windows” is the closest shipping product to a 3D GUI agent: it sees the mixed scene and acts on the spatial layout. Apple’s Voice Control is the closest action space: it can reach any labelled element, but it has no planner, so a ten-step settings change is ten spoken commands.

7.4 Research assistants and first XR GUI perception

Research systems go further, mostly in perception. GazePointAR (Lee et al., CHI 2024) fuses gaze, pointing and conversation history to resolve “this” and “that” in wearable AR, but answered only 13 of 32 participant-invented queries satisfactorily, at about 7.5 to 7.9 s per answer. RAVEN (Cao et al., CHI 2026) gives an LLM the scene graph of a Unity scene and lets it write code to answer or edit; 75.3% of 336 prompts from 8 blind and low-vision users succeeded, at 3.1 s on average. For GUI perception, Orienter (Li et al., arXiv 2409.10811) detects interactable elements in screenshots of 100 VR apps with an interactability F1 of only 46.00% (against 29.32% for the best baseline), and in GUI-World (Chen et al., ICLR 2025) XR was the hardest of six scenarios for every model. No benchmark yet measures an agent operating a headset UI.

7.5 The limits

  • Latency. LLM assistants in XR answer in about 3 to 12 s; a pinch takes well under a second. Agents pay off for multi-step or hard operations, not for single easy selections.
  • Perception. XR GUI perception is weak (F1 46%), and platforms withhold gaze and the field of view.
  • Platform access. No documented third-party API lets an agent move another app’s windows or inject input on visionOS; post hoc tools such as VRSight need a tethered PC and developer mode.
  • Agency. In VRCopilot (Zhang et al., UIST 2024), fully automatic creation lowered the user’s sense of agency compared with scaffolded creation, and some low-vision users felt an aid “feels like cheating” in games (SeeingVR). Shipping agentic flows keep a final confirmation step.

8. The catalogue: 30 operations and who should act

The dossier of this column ends with a catalogue of concrete operations on a headset or glasses, each with the techniques used today, the measured or reported difficulty, and a judgment of whether a 3D GUI agent could do it, guide the user, or neither. The judgments are our assessment, not findings of the cited works.

21 Select small targets while moving 20.4 to 36.0% errors while driving do it, with confirmation

Reading the catalogue:

  • The agent can do it when the goal is easy to state in words and the execution is expensive in 3D: placing and arranging windows, finding content behind the user, typing a query, navigating a buried setting, selecting a tiny, distant or occluded target. The costs it removes are the ones measured in section 4: depth-dependent pointing, arm fatigue, text entry at a fraction of phone speed, and multi-step menus. One utterance and one confirmation replace them.
  • The agent should guide when the user must judge the result or acquire the skill: learning gestures, fine visual alignment, safety-relevant mode changes, and travel, where spatial awareness belongs to the user.
  • Neither, yet for what is physical (fit, comfort, sickness), secret (passwords), or not perceivable (unlabelled controls in arbitrary 3D apps).

9. What this means for 3D GUI agents

  1. The cost is real, measurable, and concentrated in a few operations. Text, small or far selection, window management and buried commands account for most of the measured gap to the phone. A 3D GUI agent should be judged on those first.
  2. The action space must be richer than tap, swipe and type. The five universal tasks suggest primitives: select(target), set_pose(object, pose), place(window, anchor), travel(to), find(object), command(path), type(text). The platforms’ numeric comfort envelopes (section 3.3) and the pointing models with depth terms (section 2) can serve as constraints and as a cost model that tells the agent when to act and when to guide.
  3. The observation space is undefined. A 2D agent sees a screenshot and an accessibility tree. In XR, the user’s view is per-eye, head-dependent and private, gaze is withheld, and the accessibility tree covers 2D panels and labelled 3D entities only.
  4. Mixed initiative, not autopilot. Users accept most but not all proposals, refine after seeing results, and want to keep agency.
  5. Accessibility is the strongest near-term case. Screen readers and Voice Control already provide the action space; an agent adds the plan. VRSight’s 11% menu completion marks exactly the step an operating agent would remove.
  6. Benchmarks and human baselines are missing. No benchmark measures task success for an agent on a headset UI, and no study reports per-task human baselines (time, errors, fatigue) for whole tasks on commercial devices.

Post 4 surveys what AI agents in XR and 3D can already do and where exactly the gap lies; the research vision turns the catalogue into research questions, and the research plan follows from them.

Try it

  • In the selection lab (section 2.7), run one block with gaze + pinch and one with hand ray. Which targets does each technique fail on? Compare the throughput estimates with the slopes in the Fitts figure.
  • Switch to gaze + dwell and try to reach the far panel without passing over other buttons. How many unintended selections (Midas touch) did you make?
  • Run a block with direct touch and watch the arm-effort bar. Then run gaze + pinch: why does it stay near zero?

Exercises

  1. A settings window is 2 m away and its toggles are 2.5 cm wide. Compute their angular width. With an eye tracker of 1° accuracy and Microsoft’s 1° rule, can they be operated by gaze + pinch? How large would they have to be, and how far away could the window be placed instead?

    Hint

    $\omega = 2\arctan(0.0125/2) = 0.72°$, below both the tracker error and the 1° minimum. A 1° target at 2 m is $2 \cdot 2 \tan(0.5°) = 3.5$ cm; to make the 2.5 cm toggle cover 1°, move the window to $0.0125/\tan(0.5°) = 1.43$ m. Apple’s angular points solve the same problem by scaling the window with distance.

  2. Using the two lines of Wagner et al., $\mathrm{MT} = -0.27 + 0.88\,\mathrm{ID}$ (Handray) and $\mathrm{MT} = 0.63 + 0.35\,\mathrm{ID}$ (Gaze & Pinch), find the index of difficulty where the two techniques take the same time. For a block of 20 selections at ID 2.5, how many seconds does gaze save? Why should you not extrapolate to ID 4.6?

    Hint

    They cross at $\mathrm{ID} = 0.90 / 0.53 \approx 1.70$ bits. At ID 2.5: $1.93$ s against $1.505$ s, so about $0.43$ s per selection and $8.5$ s per block. The models were fitted on 3° targets with IDs between 1.1 and 2.6 bits; at 4.6 bits the target is smaller than the eye-tracker error, so gaze would miss rather than slow down.

  3. Write the CE computation for a user who holds a hand ray with the arm extended (shoulder load 20.5% of maximum) for 4 minutes while arranging windows. What is CE? What would CE be for the same 4 minutes with the elbow bent (12%)? What does this say about the 15% asymptote, and how would NICER differ?

    Hint

    $E(20.5) = 1236.5/5.5^{0.618} - 72.5 \approx 360$ s, so $\mathrm{CE} = 240/360 = 67\%$. At 12% the endurance is unlimited and CE is 0, although four minutes with a raised forearm is not effortless. NICER replaces Rohmert’s curve with a shoulder-specific endurance function that does not have this asymptote, and models recovery during rest.

  4. Take one task you do weekly on your phone (for example, sending a short message to a contact found by name). Break it down into the five 3D interaction tasks as it would be done on a headset, estimate the time of each step from the numbers in this post, and mark which steps an agent could do, guide or neither.

    Hint

    For example: open the app (system control, a selection at about 1 s), find the contact (symbolic input: a 6-letter search at 10 to 15 wpm takes about 5 to 7 s, plus errors), select it (selection), dictate the message, confirm. The search and the typing dominate; both are “do it with confirmation” rows of the catalogue.

  5. The adoption surveys in section 5 never offer “too hard to use” as an answer. Design a short survey or diary study that could measure whether interface complexity contributes to people stopping headset use, without leading the participants.

    Hint

    Recruit owners at purchase and follow them for months (diary entries and, with consent, usage logs). Ask open questions first (“what did you try to do last time and what happened?”), then a ranked list that includes price, comfort, content, sickness, social reasons, setup, and “I could not figure out how to do X”. Exit interviews when usage stops separate abandonment reasons from first-week friction.

Next: Agents in XR and the gap: what AI agents in XR and 3D can already perceive and do, the platforms and tooling they run on, and the gap a 3D GUI agent would fill.
entry.summary: A survey of what it costs to operate VR, AR and MR interfaces: the 3D task taxonomy, gaze, pinch, rays and touch with their pointing models, the cost of depth and the Midas touch, windows, volumes and reference frames, measured fatigue, error, text-entry and sickness numbers, adoption and accessibility evidence, the help that exists today, and a catalogue of 30 headset operations sorted by whether an agent could do them, guide them, or neither.

entry.title: GUI agents on 2D screens: a survey to November 2026

link.title: GUI agents on 2D screens: a survey to November 2026

entry.content:
Why this matters

The research vision of this column is to bring GUI agents, AI agents that operate graphical user interfaces on a user’s behalf, to the 3D interfaces of VR, AR and MR devices. Before asking what a 3D GUI agent should look like, we need an accurate picture of what 2D GUI agents already are. On phones, desktops and the web, the field moved remarkably fast: in April 2024 the best model completed 12.2% of the computer tasks in OSWorld, against 72.4% for people; by December 2025 an agent system passed the human baseline, and in 2026 frontier models ship “computer use” as a built-in skill. Almost every design decision a 3D agent will face (what to observe, how to point at a target, which actions to allow, how to train, how to evaluate, when to ask the user) has been argued over, measured and partly settled on 2D screens.

This post is a survey of that work up to November 2026. It is organized by ideas rather than by papers: the agent loop, observation, grounding, planning and memory, training, evaluation, humans and safety. For the key methods it explains how they work (inputs, outputs, training signal, loop) and gives the numbers that matter. Every section ends with what it means for 3D interfaces, and the last section collects these threads into a careful list of what transfers and what breaks. The companion posts look at the 3D side: why 3D interfaces are hard to operate and agents in XR, the platforms and the gap.

Prerequisites

  • Basic familiarity with large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs): a VLM reads images and text and writes text.
  • The idea of a Markov decision process and of policy-gradient reinforcement learning (the world models series and the embodied AI series cover both).
  • No GUI-agent background is assumed.

A note on numbers. Benchmark scores below come from papers, vendor pages and leaderboards that use different harnesses, step limits and benchmark versions, so they are only roughly comparable across sources. Each number is given with its source and date; “secondary” marks numbers known only from press or aggregators; most 2025-2026 industrial systems are technical reports on arXiv without peer review, and are marked as such.

1. What a GUI agent is

1.1 The loop

A GUI agent receives a task in natural language (“turn on Wi-Fi”, “book the cheapest flight to Osaka on Friday”) and completes it by operating the same graphical user interface (GUI) a person would use: it looks at the screen, decides what to do, and sends taps, clicks, keystrokes and scrolls. The task is therefore solved through the interface, not through a special API for each app. That is the whole point: any app that a person can use becomes usable by the agent, without the app’s developer doing anything.

Formally, an episode is a partially observable decision process. At step $t$ the agent has the instruction $g$, the current observation $o_t$ (a screenshot, a text description of the screen, or both) and its own history $h_t$ of earlier observations, thoughts and actions. A policy $\pi$ outputs an action $a_t$; the device executes it and produces the next screen $o_{t+1}$. The episode ends when the agent outputs finish, declares the task infeasible, asks the user, or runs out of steps. Success is judged on the final state of the device $s_T$:

\[a_t \sim \pi(\,\cdot \mid g,\; o_{\le t},\; a_{<t}), \qquad \text{success} = \mathbb{1}\big[\,\mathrm{check}_g(s_T) = \text{true}\,\big].\]

Inside $\pi$, most systems run some version of the loop in the figure below: observe (and possibly parse the screen into elements), plan the next step, ground it (turn “the Share button” into a concrete screen location), act, then verify or reflect on the result and update memory. Two side channels matter more than they first appear: the agent can ask the user (to resolve ambiguity or confirm a consequential action), and it can decide to stop.

Two architectural families share this loop:

  • Framework agents (2023-2024 and still common): a general LLM or VLM is prompted in each role, with hand-built perception (accessibility tree, OCR, icon detectors), memory files and sometimes several cooperating agents. AppAgent, Mobile-Agent, AutoDroid, UFO, Agent S and SeeAct are examples.
  • Native agent models (from late 2024): one VLM is trained end to end to map a screenshot plus history to a thought and an action. UI-TARS, Aguvis, OpenCUA, GUI-Owl, MAI-UI and the computer-use modes of frontier models (Claude, OpenAI’s CUA and GPT-5.x, Gemini) belong here.

The distinction is not strict: native models are often wrapped in a light framework (a planner, a reflector, a memory) and framework agents increasingly call a trained grounding model.

1.2 A short history, 2016-2026

The history falls into four phases, as the timeline shows.

UI data and UI understanding (2016-2022). HCI and mobile-systems groups mined apps at scale. ERICA (UIST 2016) and Rico (UIST 2017; 72k+ unique Android screens with view hierarchies and interaction traces) made screens into data. Models learned to caption widgets, summarize screens (Screen2Words) and embed them (Screen2Vec, UIBert). Seq2Act (ACL 2020) mapped instructions such as “turn on airplane mode” to action sequences, reaching 70.59% complete match on its PixelHelp test set. Google’s Spotlight (ICLR 2023) and Pix2Struct (ICML 2023) then showed that a model reading only the screenshot could beat models given the view hierarchy, which is often missing or wrong. Accessibility research (SUGILITE; Screen Recognition, which rebuilds accessibility metadata from pixels) contributed the idea of driving apps through, or reconstructing, accessibility information.

Reinforcement learning on synthetic UIs (2017-2022). In parallel, RL researchers built World of Bits / MiniWoB (ICML 2017), small web tasks with scripted rewards (click this button, fill this form), and MiniWoB++ (ICLR 2018), where a few demonstrations constrain exploration. AndroidEnv (2021) wrapped the Android emulator as an RL environment. DeepMind’s CC-Net (ICML 2022) reached mean human-level performance on MiniWoB++ from pixels plus DOM, but needed about 2.4 million human demonstrations: pixel-level control worked, at a data price nobody could pay for real apps.

LLM and VLM agent systems (2023-2024). With GPT-4 and GPT-4V, prompted agents appeared on every platform at once: AppAgent, Mobile-Agent, AutoDroid and MobileGPT on Android; UFO, Cradle and Agent S on desktops; MindAct, SeeAct and WebVoyager on the web. Large datasets (Android in the Wild, AITW: 715,142 episodes) and the first realistic benchmarks (Mind2Web, WebArena, OSWorld, AndroidWorld) appeared. The main lesson of this phase was that planning was not the bottleneck; grounding was.

Native models, RL at scale and commercial computer use (2024-2026). Grounding models trained on millions of synthetic elements (SeeClick, UGround, OS-Atlas) and end-to-end agent models (UI-TARS, January 2025) replaced hand-built perception. Anthropic released computer use for Claude (October 2024), OpenAI its Computer-Using Agent and Operator (January 2025), Google Gemini 2.5 Computer Use (October 2025); with GPT-5.4 (March 2026) computer use became a native skill of a general model. R1-style reinforcement learning (2025) and multi-turn online RL in thousands of parallel virtual machines pushed scores past human baselines on several benchmarks, which were then replaced by harder ones (ScreenSpot-Pro, OSWorld 2.0).

1.3 Three platforms

The loop is the same everywhere, but the three platforms differ in what the agent can see and do:

Platform Typical observation Action channel Environment for experiments
Phone (Android, iOS) screenshot, Android view hierarchy / accessibility tree tap, long press, swipe, type, back, home (via adb or an accessibility service) Android emulator snapshots (AndroidEnv, AndroidWorld), real-device farms
Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) screenshot, OS accessibility API (Windows UI Automation, macOS AX) mouse move / click / drag, keyboard, hotkeys, scroll; shell and app APIs virtual machines with snapshots (OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena)
Web screenshot, DOM, browser accessibility tree click, type, scroll, navigate, tabs (via Playwright / Chrome DevTools Protocol) self-hosted sites (WebArena), live websites (Online-Mind2Web)

Phones have small screens, touch gestures and many apps without good accessibility labels. Desktops have large, high-resolution screens with tiny targets, overlapping windows and professional software. The web has the richest structure (the DOM) but also the most adversarial content.

For 3D. The loop transfers unchanged in shape, and the success definition (a check on the final state) does too. What changes is everything inside the boxes: the observation is a viewpoint, not a screen; “ground” must produce a target in space; “act” includes continuous 6-DoF motion; and the device is a headset whose state includes the user’s body and room. Section 8 goes through each box.

2. Observation: what the agent sees

2.1 Structured observations: view hierarchies, accessibility trees and the DOM

Every GUI toolkit keeps a tree of widgets. Android exposes it as the view hierarchy and, for assistive technology, as an accessibility tree (each node has a role, a text or content description, a bounding box and flags such as clickable or checked). Windows has UI Automation, macOS the AX API, and the web has the DOM plus a browser accessibility tree. Serialized as text, the tree gives a language model exactly what it is good at: a list of named, typed elements with coordinates. The first LLM agents (DroidBot-GPT, AutoDroid, UFO, MindAct) used it, and it has clear strengths: labels are exact, invisible state (checked, disabled, off-screen items in a list) is available, and the element to act on can be named rather than located.

Its weaknesses are just as clear, and they decided the debate. Trees are missing or wrong in many apps: custom-drawn widgets, canvases, games, web apps built from divs and icon buttons without labels. They are long: the raw HTML of a modern page is far beyond what a model can read in each step, which is why MindAct (the Mind2Web baseline) first ranked candidate elements with a small model before asking the LLM. And they are platform-specific: an agent built on Android’s accessibility service does not run on Windows.

2.2 Screenshots

A screenshot is universal: every app on every platform renders pixels. A VLM turns it into visual tokens. With the patching scheme of the Qwen2.5-VL family, on which most 2025 GUI models are built, one visual token covers a 28 x 28 pixel area, so a 1080 x 2400 phone screenshot costs about $(1080/28)(2400/28) \approx 3{,}300$ tokens and a 1920 x 1080 desktop about 2,600. That is affordable, but small text and icons that occupy a few patches are hard to read; high-resolution encoders (CogAgent’s 1120 x 1120 branch), tiling (Ferret-UI’s “any resolution” sub-images) and token pruning (ShowUI) all address this.

The difficulty with pixels is not reading but pointing: a general VLM in 2023 could describe a screen well but could not say where the Save button was. Two answers emerged: give the model labels to refer to (next subsection) or teach it to output coordinates (section 3).

2.3 Set-of-Mark labels and screen parsers

Set-of-Mark (SoM) prompting (Yang et al., 2023) overlays numbered marks on segmented regions of an image so that the model can answer “17” instead of a coordinate. GUI agents adopted it at once: WebVoyager, MM-Navigator, AppAgent and Mobile-Agent draw a box and a number on each interactive element, taken from the accessibility tree when it exists or from detectors when it does not. OmniParser (Microsoft, 2024) builds the marks from pixels alone: a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector finds icons, a BLIP-2 captioner describes them, and OCR reads text. With GPT-4V, a screenshot-only OmniParser agent beat GPT-4 given the page’s HTML on Mind2Web (step success 36.5 vs 30.1 cross-website, 42.0 vs 26.4 cross-domain).

Marks have costs too: detector errors propagate, marks clutter dense screens and can hide the content they label, and SeeAct (ICML 2024) found image annotation markedly weaker than giving GPT-4V a textual list of candidate elements (offline Mind2Web step success 20.3 vs 39.1 on cross-task).

2.4 Which observation won, and why

The evidence changed with the models. The figure collects the clearest comparisons in which only the input changes.

In 2024, general models used as agents did better with text than with pixels, and best with both. What changed in 2025 is that models trained for GUIs made screenshot-only agents competitive and then dominant: UI-TARS, Aguvis, GUI-Owl, MAI-UI and the frontier computer-use modes all act from screenshots alone; GPT-5.4 reports 92.8% on Online-Mind2Web “screenshot-only” (OpenAI, March 2026). Three reasons explain the shift:

  1. Coverage. Pixels exist for every app; trees do not. An agent that needs a tree fails silently on canvases, games, remote desktops and badly labelled apps.
  2. Training data. Grounding data can be generated at scale from structure (DOM boxes rendered as screenshots, section 3), so a vision model can learn what the tree knew, then work without it.
  3. One model for all platforms. A screenshot plus generic input events (tap, click, type) is the same interface on Android, Windows and the web, which is what cross-platform native models need.

Trees did not disappear. Where they exist they remain a strong extra signal (EntWorld’s hybrid result), Windows agents such as UFO2 fuse UI Automation with vision parsing, and Apple and Google route assistant actions through app intents and accessibility APIs rather than pixels.

For 3D. The screenshot-first lesson transfers: a rendered view of the XR scene is a valid primary observation, and an XR version of OmniParser (a detector and captioner over rendered frames) is buildable. The structured side channel is even richer in 3D, because engines know every object’s name, type, pose and interactability (the scene graph), and visionOS and Android XR extend their 2D accessibility stacks to spatial apps. What breaks: a headset view is egocentric and changes with every head movement, so one UI state yields many images; the frame contains depth, stereo, occlusion and passthrough of the real world; and many immersive apps render custom 3D UI with no accessibility metadata at all, the situation Screen Recognition addressed for iOS in 2021. The agent’s “screen” also becomes a choice: the user’s view, a virtual camera placed elsewhere, or a map of the room.

3. Grounding: from “the Share button” to a screen location

3.1 The problem and its metric

GUI grounding maps a referring expression (an instruction such as “open the share menu” or a description such as “the Share icon at the bottom left”) and a screenshot to the location of the element to act on. A grounding benchmark gives $N$ triples (screenshot, instruction, target box $B_i$), the model outputs a point $\hat p_i$, and accuracy is the fraction of points inside their boxes:

\[\mathrm{Acc} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}\big[\hat p_i \in B_i\big].\]

A point is the natural output because a tap or click is a point. The metric hides an important geometric fact: whether a slightly wrong point still counts depends on the target’s size. If the prediction error is roughly Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma$ pixels in each axis, and the target is a box of half-width $a$ and half-height $b$ centred on the true point, the hit probability is

\[P(\text{hit}) = \operatorname{erf}\!\Big(\frac{a}{\sigma\sqrt2}\Big)\,\operatorname{erf}\!\Big(\frac{b}{\sigma\sqrt2}\Big).\]

For a 44 x 44 px phone icon ($a = b = 22$) and $\sigma = 8$ px this is 0.99; for a 12 px toolbar icon on a 4K professional application ($a = b = 6$) the same error gives 0.30. The same model, the same error, a very different score: this is the gap between ScreenSpot and ScreenSpot-Pro in section 3.4, and the grounding mode of the widget in section 4 lets you try it.

3.2 Three ways to output a location

  1. Choose an element from a list (mark index, element id, DOM node). Simple and exact, but only as good as the list: it needs a tree or a parser.
  2. Write coordinates as text tokens. The VLM simply outputs click(x=412, y=873). SeeClick (ACL 2024) continually pretrained Qwen-VL on about one million grounding samples to do this; UI-TARS and most later models follow, with coordinates either normalized or in absolute pixels depending on the base model. It needs no parser, but a coordinate written as digits receives weak spatial supervision (an answer one pixel off is as “wrong” to the cross-entropy loss as one a screen away) and gives a single brittle point with no confidence.
  3. Predict a heatmap. GUI-Actor (NeurIPS 2025) adds an <ACTOR> token whose attention over the visual patches is the output: every patch overlapping the target box is supervised, the peak is the click, and a small verifier ranks candidate regions. The spread of the map is a natural confidence signal.

3.3 The grounding models

The table lists the models that shaped the area. Scores are on ScreenSpot (SS), its corrected version ScreenSpot-v2 (SS-v2) and the professional, high-resolution ScreenSpot-Pro (SS-Pro), as reported by the paper or model card cited.

Model (first version) What is new Data / base Reported grounding
SeeClick (Jan 2024; ACL 2024) Grounding pretraining; introduced ScreenSpot ~1M samples on Qwen-VL SS 53.4 (CogAgent 47.4, GPT-4V 16.2)
CogAgent (Dec 2023; CVPR 2024) 1120 x 1120 high-resolution cross-attention branch 18B; CCS400K screenshots SS 47.4
Ferret-UI (Apr 2024; ECCV 2024) “Any resolution” sub-images for tall screens and small widgets Apple; mobile UI tasks Android grounding 83.5 vs GPT-4V 4.7 (its own tasks)
OmniParser (Aug 2024) Pixel-only parser: icon detector + captioner + OCR, marks for any VLM YOLOv8, BLIP-2 SS 73.0 with GPT-4V
UGround (Oct 2024; ICLR 2025) Pure-vision grounder trained on synthetic web elements ~10M elements, 1.3M screenshots SS 77.7 / 86.3 / 89.4 (2B / 7B / 72B, Qwen2-VL)
OS-Atlas (Oct 2024; ICLR 2025) Cross-platform grounding corpus; introduced SS-v2 13.58M elements, 5 platforms SS 82.47 (7B); SS-Pro 18.9
ShowUI (Nov 2024; CVPR 2025) UI-guided visual token selection (fewer tokens) 2B lightweight vision-language-action model
Aria-UI (Dec 2024; ACL 2025) Mixture-of-experts grounder using action history as context MoE context-aware grounding
UI-TARS (Jan 2025) / UI-TARS-1.5 (Apr 2025) Native agent model; RL-trained 1.5 Qwen2-VL; ByteDance SS-Pro 38.1 (72B) / 61.6 (1.5)
Jedi (May 2025; NeurIPS 2025 D&B) UI decomposition and synthesis; OSWorld-G benchmark 4M synthetic examples o3 + Jedi lifts OSWorld 23% to 51%
GUI-Actor (Jun 2025; NeurIPS 2025) Coordinate-free attention head + verifier Qwen2.5-VL-7B SS-v2 92.1 (92.5 w/ verifier); SS-Pro 44.6 (47.7)
UI-Venus (Aug 2025) RL fine-tuning with point-in-box reward 7B / 72B SS-Pro 61.9 (72B)
Ferret-UI Lite (Sep 2025) 3B on-device agent Apple SS-v2 91.6; SS-Pro 53.3
Holo2 (Nov 2025, blog) Open localization models from H Company Qwen3-VL SS-Pro 66.1 (30B-A3B)
UI-Venus-2 (Aug 2026) Verified tasks across 170+ apps 27B SS-Pro 74.1
GroundCascade (Nov 2026) Cascade: a second grounder only when the first is unsure system of models SS-Pro 85.33

All entries without a venue are arXiv technical reports. The progression has a clear logic: first teach a VLM to point at all (SeeClick, CogAgent), then scale the data synthetically (UGround, OS-Atlas, Jedi), then change the output head (GUI-Actor), then train with reinforcement learning on cheap rule-based rewards (section 5.3), and finally spend more computation at test time on the hard cases (section 3.5).

3.4 ScreenSpot versus ScreenSpot-Pro: the grounding gap

ScreenSpot (600+ screenshots, 1.2k+ instructions on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and web) quickly saturated above 90%. ScreenSpot-Pro (K. Li et al., April 2025; ACM MM 2025) moved to 23 professional applications in five industries on three operating systems: CAD, video editing, scientific and office software on high-resolution screens, where targets are tiny and similar-looking. At release the best model scored 18.9%.

Panel (a) shows the gap: the same models lose 30-60 points when the targets become small and the screens large and dense. Panel (b) shows how the gap closed. Single-pass accuracy rose from 18.9% (April 2025) through 61.6% (UI-TARS-1.5, April 2025) and 67.9% (MAI-UI, December 2025) to 74.1% (UI-Venus-2-27B, August 2026). GUI-Owl-1.5 reports 80.3% (February 2026) without stating the inference setting in its abstract.

3.5 Look, then zoom: search and cascades

ScreenSpot-Pro’s own paper proposed ScreenSeekeR, a training-free procedure in which a planner model proposes the region where the target should be, the grounder searches that crop, and the search recurses: 48.1% without any training, against 18.9% for the best single pass. The lesson, that reducing the search area helps more than a bigger model, was absorbed into later models as an explicit zoom step (GUI-ARP’s adaptive region perception; MAI-UI’s zoom mode, 73.5% vs 67.9% single pass; Qwen-UI-Agent 81.5% with zoom) and into iterative refinement (Chain-of-Ground, 68.4%). GroundCascade (November 2026) asks a second grounder only when the first one’s prediction looks unreliable, and reaches 85.33%.

Look-then-zoom is the 2D version of what a headset does with foveated rendering and gaze: spend resolution where the target is likely to be. It is also a reminder that test-time computation (section 4.6) works for perception as well as for planning.

3.6 Split the planner from the grounder

If grounding is the bottleneck, one option is to let a strong general model plan and a specialist ground. SeeAct (ICML 2024) measured the bottleneck directly on live websites: GPT-4V completed 51.1% of tasks when a human did the grounding (“oracle”), but only 37.8% with the best automatic grounding. Jedi showed the other direction: OpenAI’s o3 as planner went from 23% to 51% on OSWorld when its clicks were grounded by the 7B Jedi model. Agent S2 (2025) pushed the idea to a mixture of grounders (visual, textual and structural specialists chosen per target), and Phi-Ground (2025) studied the training of such specialist grounders systematically.

For 3D. Grounding transfers better than any other part, and in some ways gets easier: the best 2D grounders already output heatmaps (GUI-Actor) or zoom in two passes, which map directly to ray casting through the heatmap peak and to gaze-guided foveation; and synthetic grounding data, generated in 2D from the DOM, can be generated in 3D from the engine, which can render any object from any viewpoint with an exact label. What breaks: the output is no longer a pixel but an object or a volume. One pixel can correspond to several objects at different depths; small, distant or edge-on targets project to a few pixels (the ScreenSpot-Pro problem, made worse by headset optics); targets can be occluded or outside the field of view; and instructions are often relative to the user’s body (“the panel on my left”). Section 8.2 makes this concrete.

4. Planning, reflection and memory

4.1 Reasoning before acting

Almost all agents write a short thought before each action, in the ReAct style: “The Wi-Fi switch is off; tap it” followed by tap(...). AitZ (2024) annotated Android episodes with chain-of-action-thought (what the screen shows, what the action should achieve, what happened), and UI-TARS trained its native model on “System-2” reasoning traces that include task decomposition, reflection and milestone recognition. Reasoning helps planning; for pure grounding it can hurt: GUI-G1 (2025) found that long chains of thought lower grounding accuracy, and many grounders answer with coordinates directly.

4.2 The action space

The action space is a design decision with large effects. A typical mobile action space is tap(x, y), long_press(x, y), swipe(start, end), type(text), back, home, wait, plus three non-device actions: finish, infeasible (the task cannot be done here; MoTIF, ECCV 2022, made this a research question) and ask_user(question). Desktop agents add mouse moves, drags, scrolling, keyboard shortcuts and window management.

Panel (a) of the design-lever figure shows how much this choice matters: AppAgent’s success rose from 2.2% with raw actions to 48.9% with a small action space over numbered elements, before any other improvement. Agent S (ICLR 2025) generalized the point into the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI): design the interface for the agent (a constrained, grounded action set with immediate feedback) rather than force it through the human one.

The strongest recent systems mix GUI actions with programmatic ones. UFO2 (2025) calls a native application API when one exists and falls back to GUI clicks when it does not; CoAct-1 (2025) lets an orchestrator choose between a GUI operator and a programmer agent that writes scripts, reaching 60.76% on OSWorld; UI-TARS-2 and Qwen-UI-Agent (2026) unify GUI, terminal (CLI) and file-system actions; MAI-UI adds Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls and explicit user interaction to the action space. MobileWorld (2025) turned asking the user and MCP tools into scored task types. A cross-interface authorization study (2026) draws the security conclusion: consent should be tied to the effect of an action, whether it is issued through a click, a command line or an API.

4.3 Reflection and verification

A single wrong tap can send an agent into the wrong app; what separates good agents from bad ones is whether they notice. Mobile-Agent-v2 (NeurIPS 2024) added a reflection agent that compares the screens before and after each action and classifies the action as correct, erroneous (wrong page: go back) or ineffective (nothing changed: try something else); together with a planning agent that keeps a task-progress summary and a memory unit for focus content, it raised success on its benchmark from 43.2% (v1) to 75.0%. UI-TARS uses reflection tuning: mistakes found in its own online traces are paired with corrections, and the model is trained on the corrected continuations, so recovery becomes part of the policy.

Verification can also choose between candidates. GTA1 (ICLR 2026) samples several plans and lets a judge pick one. Agent S3 (2025; TMLR 2026) scales this to whole episodes with Behavior Best-of-N: run several complete rollouts, turn each into a short “behaviour narrative” of what changed on screen, and let a judge compare the narratives. This gave 72.6% on OSWorld, the first published result above the 72.36% human baseline (December 2025).

The negative result is equally important: the failure analysis of OSWorld 2.0 (June 2026) says that agents still “lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification”.

4.4 Memory and exploration

Agents need two kinds of memory. Within a task, they must track progress and remember information read on one screen and needed on another (Mobile-Agent-v2’s memory unit, Mobile-Agent-v3’s notetaker). Across tasks, they can accumulate knowledge about apps:

  • Exploration documents. AppAgent first lets the agent explore an app (or watch a human), then writes a document describing what each element does. Its success rose from 48.9% to 73.3% with self-explored documents, 84.4% with demonstration-based ones and 95.6% with manual documentation (design-lever figure, panel a).
  • UI transition graphs. AutoDroid (MobiCom 2024) explores apps offline without an LLM, builds a graph of which action leads to which screen, and turns it into prompt hints at run time: 71.3% task success with GPT-4 on its DroidTask benchmark, and 51.7% lower query cost.
  • Reusable skills. MobileGPT stores sub-tasks; Agent Workflow Memory (ICML 2025) induces reusable workflows from past episodes (+24.6% and +51.1% relative on Mind2Web and WebArena); Mobile-Agent-E (2025) writes “Tips” and “Shortcuts” after each task (+22% absolute on Mobile-Eval-E); AppAgentX compresses repeated action chains into new high-level actions. Agent S4 (October 2026) goes furthest: a meta-agent evolves the agent’s own tools, scripts and usage knowledge, and with a 27B open model reaches 21.3% on OSWorld V2 (3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces).

4.5 Multi-agent designs

Several systems split the work among role agents. Mobile-Agent-v2 uses planning, decision and reflection agents; Mobile-Agent-E adds a manager and a perceptor; Mobile-Agent-v3 wraps the GUI-Owl model in manager, worker, reflector and notetaker roles. On desktops, UFO’s HostAgent decomposes a task and dispatches per-application AppAgents; Agent S2 combines a generalist planner with specialist grounders; Magentic-One’s orchestrator keeps task and progress ledgers and directs a web surfer, a file surfer, a coder and a terminal. UFO3 (2025) orchestrates agents across Windows, Linux and Android devices. Minitap’s five-role system (planning, sub-goal tracking, state capture, decision, execution) reports pass@3 of 100% on AndroidWorld, and losing its task decomposition costs it 26.1 points.

The price of roles is latency: each role is another model call, and OSWorld-Human (2025) found that planning, reflection and judging calls dominate the time agents take.

4.6 Test-time scaling and look-ahead

When the environment can be reset, an agent can try several things and keep the best: Best-of-N rollouts (Agent S3), sampled plans with a judge (GTA1), or best-first tree search over web states (Koh et al., 2024; 26.4% on VisualWebArena). When it cannot, a world model can imagine the outcome of candidate actions: WebDreamer lets the LLM simulate what each candidate click would show and scores the predictions, at 4-5 times the efficiency of tree search on live sites (section 5.5).

4.7 Try it: one agent, three observations, one slip

The widget runs three scripted episodes on a toy phone. Step through them and switch the observation between the screenshot, Set-of-Mark labels and the accessibility tree: the thought stays the same, but the action is written as coordinates, as a mark number or as a node name. The photo episode contains a grounding slip (the agent aims at the small Share icon and hits Edit), a reflection step that notices the wrong screen and goes back, and a confirmation request before a message is sent. The Grounding mode lets you place the model’s predicted point yourself and add Gaussian error, to see why small targets punish a few pixels of error.

A GUI agent episode, step by step. Choose an episode (top row), the observation type (Screenshot, Set-of-Mark or A11y tree) and step with Next / Prev. Each step shows what the agent sees, its one-line thought and its action (red crosshair for taps, blue box for typing, the highlighted back key, a dialog when it asks the user); the next step shows the resulting screen. In the photo episode, step 3 is a grounding slip and step 4 a reflection that recovers. Grounding mode (or tap the phone): drag the predicted point; dashed boxes are the clickable elements, dots are 400 samples of a Gaussian error of the chosen sigma (green: same element, orange: another element, grey: empty space).

For 3D. Reflection on outcomes (did the panel actually open?), persistent shortcuts and exploration documents transfer directly; exploration-then-document is how an agent could learn an unfamiliar XR app before a user needs it. The hybrid action space is natural on XR platforms, where Apple and Google already expose app intents and function calling to their assistants. What breaks: exploration in 3D can move or delete content in the user’s space, so it must run in a sandboxed copy; best-of-N over full rollouts is impossible on the user’s live surroundings without a simulated twin; and multi-agent prompting multiplies latency, which a headset wearer feels more than a phone user.

5. Training GUI agents

By 2026 most strong agents follow a four-stage recipe: collect or synthesize data, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding and trajectories, reinforcement learning on grounding with rule-based rewards, and online multi-turn RL in many parallel environments. World models appear at several points. The figure maps the stages.

5.1 Data

Human demonstrations came first. AITW (NeurIPS 2023) collected 715,142 Android episodes over 30,378 instructions; AndroidControl (NeurIPS 2024) collected 15,283 demonstrations over 833 apps with both high-level and step-level instructions, and gave a sobering result: in-domain performance scales with data, but performance on unseen apps grows much more slowly. OpenCUA (2025) released AgentNet, desktop demonstrations across three operating systems and 200+ applications, with its annotation tool.

Demonstrations are expensive, so most data is now synthesized:

  • From tutorials. Synatra turns indirect knowledge (how-to articles) into about 100K demonstrations at roughly USD 0.031 each; AgentTrek replays web tutorials with a VLM agent at about USD 0.55 per trajectory; TongUI builds 143K trajectories from multimodal tutorials; Explorer generates 94K at about USD 0.28; Fara-7B’s FaraGen pipeline produces verified trajectories for about USD 1 each.
  • From exploration. OS-Genesis (ACL 2025) inverts the usual order. Instead of writing a task and trying to execute it, it explores first (rule-based clicks, typing, scrolling), then asks GPT-4o to describe each observed transition as a low-level instruction and to compose them into high-level tasks (“reverse task synthesis”), re-executes them and filters the trajectories with a reward model. With about a thousand such trajectories, Qwen2-VL-7B reached 17.41% on AndroidWorld against 6.25% with task-first synthesis.
  • Grounding labels from structure. UGround rendered web pages and used their DOM to label about 10 million elements; OS-Atlas built 13.58 million across five platforms; Jedi decomposed interfaces into widget types and synthesized 4 million examples. This is the data path that matters most for 3D, where the engine plays the role of the DOM.

5.2 Supervised fine-tuning

The common SFT recipe trains grounding first, then acting. Aguvis (ICML 2025) makes the two stages explicit: a grounding stage on single-step (instruction, screenshot, point) data, then a planning-and-reasoning stage on multi-step trajectories with inner monologue. UI-TARS adds large perception datasets (element captioning, dense screen description, state transitions), a unified cross-platform action space, reasoning traces and reflection tuning. The result of SFT is a capable but brittle policy: it imitates the paths in its data and has never experienced its own mistakes.

5.3 Reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards

In early 2025 the “R1” recipe from reasoning models (Group Relative Policy Optimization, GRPO, with verifiable rewards) reached GUIs, first for grounding and single-step actions. For a training example, the model samples $G$ answers $o_1, \dots, o_G$ and each gets a reward $r_i$. GRPO needs no value network: each answer’s advantage is its reward standardized within the group,

\[A_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)},\]

and the policy is pushed towards answers with positive advantage (with a clipped probability ratio and a KL penalty to the reference model, as in PPO). For grounding the reward is a rule, not a learned model:

\[r = r_{\text{format}} + \mathbb{1}\big[\hat p \in B\big] \quad\text{or}\quad r = r_{\text{format}} + \mathrm{IoU}(\hat B, B).\]

Because the reward is exact and free, a few thousand examples suffice. UI-R1 (March 2025) used 136 tasks to improve a 3B model by 22.1 points on ScreenSpot and 6.0 on ScreenSpot-Pro; GUI-R1 beat OS-Atlas with about 3K samples; SE-GUI reached 47.3% on ScreenSpot-Pro with 3K samples (7B). Two refinements address the obvious problems of a 0/1 point reward. GUI-G1 found reward hacking when the model predicts boxes (predicting huge boxes raises IoU-style rewards cheaply) and added a box-size constraint. GUI-G² replaced the binary hit with Gaussian rewards, a smooth score that is highest at the element’s centre and spreads with the element’s size, so that “almost right” is rewarded more than “far off”.

5.4 Online multi-turn reinforcement learning

Single-step rewards do not teach recovery or long-horizon planning. For that the agent must act in a live environment and be rewarded at the end of an episode. DigiRL (NeurIPS 2024) was the first convincing demonstration on real Android apps: start from offline RL on existing data, then continue online in parallel emulators with advantage-weighted updates, an automatic curriculum and a VLM that judges success. A 1.3B model went from 17.7% to 67.2% on AitW tasks, ahead of CogAgent (38.5%) and filtered behaviour cloning (57.8%). WebRL (ICLR 2025) generated new tasks from the agent’s failures and trained an outcome reward model, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 4.8% to 42.4% on WebArena-Lite.

In 2025-2026 this became an infrastructure race:

System Environment scale Notes

ComputerRL (Aug 2025) thousands of VMs API-GUI actions, alternating RL and SFT; OSWorld 48.9% (9B)

A careful 2026 study (Gu et al.) adds the caveat: with the same algorithm, RL gains shrink as test tasks move away from training. For UI-TARS-7B-SFT the gain was +17.5 points on unseen instances of training tasks, +11.1 on unseen task templates and +4.2 on unseen applications; for Qwen3-VL-8B, +10.3, +7.4 and +0. A few steps of adaptation inside the target app recovered +22.9.

5.5 World models for GUIs

A world model predicts the next observation given the current one and an action. For GUIs it has three uses: look-ahead before acting, an imagined environment for RL, and data synthesis. The representations differ:

  • Text. WMA (ICLR 2025) predicts a natural-language description of what changes after an action and uses it to choose actions on WebArena and Mind2Web without training the policy; WebDreamer lets the LLM itself imagine each candidate’s outcome.
  • Code. Code2World (2026) predicts the next screen as renderable HTML, which keeps text and layout exact; plugged into Gemini-2.5-Flash it adds 9.5% on AndroidWorld. Generative Visual Code Mobile World Models (ICML 2026) do the same for mobile.
  • Pixels. ViMo generates the next screenshot with text placeholders; NeuralOS (ICLR 2026) simulates a whole desktop with a recurrent state tracker and a diffusion renderer.
  • For training. DynaWeb and WM-R1 (2026) train policies inside imagined rollouts, and WebWorld scales a web simulator to over a million interactions.

These are the GUI counterparts of the video and 3D world models discussed in the world models series.

For 3D. The recipe transfers, and parts of it become easier. A ray-collider test is an exact, free grounding reward, so R1-style grounding RL for spatial targets can be bootstrapped from engine data with no human labels; reverse task synthesis fits engines well, since random exploration produces state transitions that a VLM can describe as tasks; and predicting a scene-description delta (a USD or glTF transform change) is the 3D analogue of Code2World’s HTML. What breaks: there is no XR trajectory corpus at all (no AITW, no AndroidControl), XR simulators need a GPU per instance, which makes 20,000 parallel environments expensive, and the generalization study warns that RL gains may not survive the move to unseen XR apps, which share far fewer widget conventions than phone apps.

6. Evaluation and the state of the art

6.1 Offline, online and live evaluation

Early datasets were evaluated offline: at each step, does the agent’s action match the recorded human action? AITW counts a tap as correct if it falls within 14% of the screen distance or inside the (enlarged) element box. Offline step accuracy is cheap and reproducible but misleading: any valid alternative path counts as an error, and high step accuracy does not imply that whole tasks succeed. Online, execution-based benchmarks run the agent in a real environment and check the final state with a program. Live-web benchmarks run on real websites and use a judge, because the web cannot be reset.

6.2 Progress over time

The OSWorld curve is the clearest summary of the field: 12.24% at release (April 2024), 14.9% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet with computer use (October 2024; 22.0% with more steps), 38.1% for OpenAI’s CUA (January 2025), 61.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 on OSWorld-Verified (September 2025), 72.6% for Agent S3 (December 2025), 75.0% for GPT-5.4 (March 2026) and 78.7% for GPT-5.5 (April 2026), with industrial models around 80% by mid-2026 and 83.4% reported for Claude Opus 4.8 by secondary sources. That is roughly a 6.5-fold increase in two years. The long-horizon OSWorld 2.0 then reset the scale to about 20%.

Why should longer tasks collapse so sharply? A back-of-the-envelope model helps. If each step succeeds independently with probability $q$ and a task needs $n$ steps, the task succeeds with probability $q^n$. With $q = 0.99$, a 30-step task (the scale of OSWorld 1.0) succeeds 74% of the time; a 318-step task (the average number of tool calls in OSWorld 2.0) succeeds 4% of the time. Real agents recover from some errors, so this is pessimistic, but it explains why verification and recovery, not single-step accuracy, decide long tasks.
