Apple’s route at WWDC 2026 was App Intents rather than pixel control.

6.4 How far to trust the numbers

The 2D literature learned several lessons about evaluation the hard way:

  1. Offline overstates. Online-Mind2Web, “An Illusion of Progress?” (COLM 2025), found that many web agents that looked strong on earlier benchmarks did not beat the 2024 SeeAct baseline on live tasks.
  2. Evaluators have bugs. OSWorld-Verified (July 2025) fixed more than 300 issues, mostly in evaluation scripts; scores before and after are not directly comparable. Harness, step limit and thinking budget move scores by several points.
  3. Self-reporting and saturation. The AndroidWorld leaderboard lists several self-reported 100% entries and marks the benchmark saturated; ScreenSpot, ScreenSpot-v2 and WebVoyager are saturated too.
  4. Reliability is not capability. If one attempt succeeds with probability $p$, the chance that at least one of $k$ attempts succeeds is $\text{pass@}k = 1-(1-p)^k$, while the chance that all $k$ succeed is $\text{pass}^k = p^k$. With $p = 0.9$ and $k = 3$ these are 0.999 and 0.729. A user needs the second. Minitap reports both on AndroidWorld: pass@3 100%, pass^3 94.0%.
  5. Efficiency. OSWorld-Human (2025) found that the best agents take 2.7 to 4.3 times more steps than necessary, that later steps take up to three times longer than early ones, and that tasks take tens of minutes.
  6. Judges are noisy. WebVoyager’s GPT-4V judge and Online-Mind2Web’s WebJudge agree with people about 85% of the time.

For 3D. The benchmark design transfers: resettable environments, parameterized tasks with programmatic checks (AndroidWorld), held-out apps, reliability (pass^k) and efficiency metrics, and human-validated judges. What breaks: resettable VMs become XR simulators or engine builds that must run headless and in parallel on GPUs; success checks need spatial tolerances (placed within 5 cm, facing the user); a judge looking at one rendered frame cannot see an occluded result; and testing on real devices involves a person’s body and room. The only XR material in the 2D benchmark literature is GUI-World’s 393 screen recordings of VR, AR and MR interfaces, evaluated as video question answering (GPT-4o 84.3% on multiple choice). No interactive benchmark in which an agent operates an XR interface appears in the 2D literature; post 4 looks at what exists on the XR side.

7. Humans in the loop, accessibility, safety and privacy

7.1 Delegation, oversight and asking

An agent acting for a person must decide when to involve them. Morae (UIST 2025) studied this with blind and low-vision (BLV) users, for whom silent choices are invisible: in a formative study, an agent reported “completed” for 484 of 576 feasible requests but only 189 were correct, and 182 failures involved ambiguity (which flight, which size). Morae detects decision points, pauses, and generates an accessible choice interface. On tasks that require a pause it succeeded 65.6% of the time against 50.8% for OpenAI’s Operator, and in a study with 10 BLV participants users completed more tasks with it, at the cost of slower runs.

How often to ask is a scheduling problem. “When Should Users Check?” (CHI 2026) modelled confirmation frequency in multi-step tasks; 81% of its 48 participants preferred intermediate confirmations over confirming only at the end, and the scheduled confirmations cut task time by 13.54%. Other 2026 work compares oversight strategies in live sessions (48 participants, 192 sessions), predicts when real users intervene (CowCorpus), and designs for the short “micro-waits” during agent runs. A usability study of Operator and Manus (CAIS 2026) found a wide gap between industry aspirations and what users could actually get done.

Not every user wants the agent to act. Context-aware guidance for screen-reader users (CHI 2026) helps people operate software themselves, and “Beyond Chat and Clicks” (2026) has the agent transform the live interface around the user instead of clicking through it. These “guide me” and “reshape the UI” modes are an alternative to full autonomy.

7.2 Accessibility

GUI agents are often promoted as an accessibility technology, but they are themselves inaccessible in revealing ways. The A11y-CUA dataset (CHI 2026) found that a computer-use agent that succeeds on 78.3% of tasks drops to 41.67% when restricted to keyboard-only interaction and to 28.3% with a screen magnifier, the settings many disabled users rely on. On 1,258 real desktop commands from eight blind users, GPT-5 succeeded 52.5% of the time (EMNLP 2026). ElderBench (2026) collects 249 tasks elicited from older adults.

7.3 Security: everything on the screen is input

A GUI agent reads whatever is displayed, so every pixel is an input channel, including content written by attackers. The attacks are effective:

  • Pop-ups. Adversarial pop-ups on OSWorld and VisualWebArena reached 86% attack success and cut task success by 47%; telling the agent to ignore pop-ups did not help (ACL 2025).
  • Injected page content. EIA steals specific personal data in up to 70% of cases (ICLR 2025); perturbing under 5% of a page’s pixels hijacks agents in up to 67% (ICLR 2025).
  • Visual prompt injection. VPI-Bench reaches up to 51% on computer-use agents and 100% on browser agents (ICLR 2026); RedTeamCUA aims web injections at operating-system actions and finds that more capable agents can be more exploitable (ICLR 2026); StepJack spreads an injection over several steps and raises success from 41.7% to 72.9% (2026).
  • Adaptive attacks. Against 21 defence configurations, adaptive visual injection still succeeds about 92% of the time (November 2026).

Harm benchmarks measure the other side: OS-Harm (NeurIPS 2025) tests misuse, injection and misbehaviour on 150 OSWorld tasks; MobileSafetyBench does the same on Android; SEAM (2026) splits harmful tasks across screens and finds agents complete up to 92% of them.

Shipped defences are layered rather than perfect. OpenAI’s Operator system card reports a confirmation recall of 92% on 607 tasks, a prompt-injection monitor with 99% recall and 90% precision, and an injection susceptibility of 23% with mitigations against 62% without. Google’s Gemini Computer Use attaches a safety decision (allowed, requires confirmation, blocked) to each proposed action. Anthropic recommends a minimal-privilege VM and confirmation of consequential actions. Microsoft’s Windows agent workspace and UFO2’s picture-in-picture desktop isolate the agent from the user’s session.

7.4 Privacy

Screenshots contain everything on screen. PriMobiBench (ACM CCS 2026) found that VLM-driven mobile agents can extract sensitive on-screen data in up to 82.5% of cases and infer user profiles about 70% of the time; masking task-irrelevant parts of the interface cut profiling by up to 58% at about 8% task-performance cost.

For 3D. Pause on ambiguity, scheduled confirmation, confirmation of consequential actions, takeover for credentials and guide-instead-of-do modes all transfer, and spatial references (“put it over there”) make ambiguity more frequent than in 2D. What breaks: confirmation and takeover must work without mouse and keyboard and without breaking presence; an agent that moves content in the user’s space can startle them or move something they are reaching for; passthrough brings uncontrolled real-world text (posters, screens, signs) into the agent’s input, which enlarges the injection surface that 2D defences already fail to close; and headset cameras, eye tracking and room scans are far more sensitive than screenshots.

8. From 2D to 3D: what transfers and what breaks

This section collects the “For 3D” notes into one argument. The question is not whether ideas from 2D agents are useful in XR (they clearly are) but which assumptions of 2D agents fail, because those failures define the research problems of a 3D GUI agent.

8.1 Observation

A 2D agent’s observation is a screenshot that is the same for the user and the agent. In a headset there are several candidate observations, and none is agreed: the stereo frames the user sees, a monocular rendering, depth, the engine’s scene graph, the platform’s accessibility information for spatial apps, the head, hand and gaze poses of the user, or a rendered “agent view” from a viewpoint the agent chooses. The 2D lesson (pixels for coverage, structure where available) suggests a hybrid, but the viewpoint problem is new: one UI state produces a different image every time the user moves.

8.2 Grounding in depth

The figure contrasts the two settings with a real visibility computation.

A 2D grounder outputs a pixel. A 3D grounder must output a target object (or a point on it), and the natural way to get there from a 2D model is to cast a ray. If the model predicts pixel $(u, v)$ in a view with intrinsics $K$, camera rotation $R$ and position $\mathbf c$, the ray is

\[\mathbf x(t) = \mathbf c + t\,\frac{R K^{-1} [u, v, 1]^\top}{\lVert R K^{-1} [u, v, 1]^\top \rVert}, \qquad t > 0,\]

and the target is the first collider it hits. A pixel error becomes an angular error of about $\delta/f$ radians for focal length $f$ in pixels, and a lateral error of about $z\,\delta/f$ at distance $z$: for a 1920-pixel-wide view with a 90° horizontal field of view, $f = 960$ px, so a 10 px error at 2 m is about 2 cm, enough to miss a small button on a far panel. A heatmap output (GUI-Actor) is better than a point here, because its spread can be turned into a cone of rays and compared with the sizes of the candidate objects. Occlusion adds a failure that 2D grounding never had: the ray may hit a nearer object (panel B in the figure), and the right action may be to move the head or the panel first.

8.3 Action space

2D actions are a handful of discrete types over 2D points. XR input includes ray-and-pinch selection, direct touch, grab-and-place with a full 6-DoF pose (a rotation and a translation, an element of $SE(3)$), rotation and scaling, two-handed gestures, gaze-and-pinch, gaze dwell, voice, controller buttons, and locomotion or teleportation. Many of these have no “click” equivalent, and their success is judged with tolerances (aligned within a few degrees, placed within a few centimetres). Language models are poor at producing such sequences directly: on ComboBench (2025), the best model mapped VR game actions to the exact controller and headset sequences only 11.7% of the time. The 2D answer, a small designed action space plus APIs where possible (AppAgent, Agent S’s ACI, UFO2), is probably the right starting point, with deterministic low-level controllers below the language model, as ClawMobile (2026) argues for phones.

8.4 Targets outside the view

A 2D agent handles hidden content by scrolling, switching tabs and opening menus, and memory helps it remember what it has seen. In XR, a window can be behind the user, occluded by a real or virtual object, or in another room, and the user moves. The agent needs to decide where to look (or ask the user to turn), and it needs a persistent spatial memory of where windows and objects are, which is a scene graph with anchors rather than a list of screens. Spatial memory is a known weakness of current multimodal models: on VSI-Bench (2024), the best model scored 45.4% against about 79% for people on spatial questions about indoor videos.

8.5 Latency

On a desktop, an agent that takes three seconds per step and twenty minutes per task can run in the background while the user does something else. In a headset the user is inside the interface, watching. The figure puts the numbers side by side: per-step times of 2D agents are two orders of magnitude above what real-time 3D game agents achieve, and the first XR prototypes are slower still. The 2D toolbox (quantization, which cut UI-TARS-2’s per-round latency from 4.0 s to 2.5 s at a cost of 3.1 OSWorld points; speculative multi-action planning in UFO2; batched actions; small on-device models such as Ferret-UI Lite and Fara-7B; MAI-UI’s device-cloud routing) all applies, but a headset also has a hard rendering budget of 8-14 ms per frame on the same chip, and VideoGameBench (2025) shows that agents that do well when a game pauses for them do far worse in real time, while XR cannot pause. Designs that split work (the headset perceives and renders, a phone or the cloud plans) and that guide the user while the agent thinks are likely to be necessary.

8.6 Data and evaluation

The 2D field was built on data: Rico, AITW, AndroidControl, Mind2Web, and millions of synthetic grounding labels. For XR there is no instruction-to-action trajectory corpus, the largest public VR UI-element dataset has about 17.7K frames (DISCOVR, UIST 2025), and no interactive benchmark exists in which an agent must operate an XR app to complete a task. Building one means solving the problems of section 6.4 in 3D: headless, resettable XR runtimes, success checks with spatial tolerances, held-out apps and reliability metrics. Post 4 reviews the platforms and tools that could host such a benchmark, and post 3 explains, from the human side, which 3D interactions are hard enough that delegating them is worth it.

8.7 What this means for the column

Three conclusions carry forward into the research vision and the research plan:

  1. Most of the agent stack can be reused. Screenshot-first native models, planner/grounder splits, reflection, exploration memory, hybrid action spaces, the SFT-then-RL recipe and execution-based evaluation are mature and open (UI-TARS, GUI-Owl, OpenCUA, MAI-UI weights and code).
  2. The new problems are spatial. Viewpoint-dependent observation, grounding with depth and occlusion, off-view targets with spatial memory, a continuous 6-DoF action space, and latency inside the interface have no 2D counterpart that solves them.
  3. The missing pieces are infrastructure. A trajectory dataset, a grounding benchmark for spatial targets and an interactive, execution-checked benchmark for XR apps would play the role that Rico, ScreenSpot and OSWorld played in 2D.

Summary

  • A GUI agent turns an instruction into actions on the same interface a person uses, through a loop of observe, plan, ground, act, verify and remember; native models now do the first four in one VLM.
  • Screenshots won over accessibility trees as the primary observation because they cover every app and because grounding data can be synthesized from structure; trees remain a useful extra signal.
  • Grounding was the 2024 bottleneck. Synthetic data, heatmap heads, rule-reward RL and zoom/cascade inference raised ScreenSpot-Pro from 18.9% (April 2025) to 74% single pass and 85% with a cascade (November 2026).
  • Action-space design, exploration documents, reflection and best-of-N selection each moved success by tens of points with the model held fixed.
  • Training is SFT on human and synthetic trajectories, then GRPO with rule rewards, then online multi-turn RL in thousands to tens of thousands of environments; gains shrink on unseen apps.
  • OSWorld passed the human baseline in December 2025 and frontier models ship computer use natively; long-horizon OSWorld 2.0 (best 20.6%) shows what remains: tracking constraints, asking, verifying.
  • Every pixel is an attack surface; adaptive injections defeat current defences, and products rely on confirmation, monitoring and isolation.
  • For 3D, the stack transfers but observation, grounding, action, field of view, latency, data and evaluation each break in specific ways, which define the research agenda of this column.

Representative papers

Learning resources

  • Surveys: Large Language Model-Brained GUI Agents: A Survey (C. Zhang et al., 2024, arXiv), the most complete roadmap; OS Agents: A Survey on MLLM-based Agents for General Computing Devices Use (X. Hu et al., ACL 2025, arXiv); Reinforcement Learning in GUI Agents: A Survey Toward Digital Inhabitants (J. Hu et al., TMLR 2026, arXiv).
  • Environments to run yourself: AndroidWorld (Android emulator tasks), OSWorld (desktop VMs), WebArena (self-hosted sites).
  • Open agents and models: Agent S, UI-TARS, OmniParser, OpenCUA.
  • Vendor documentation worth reading for the safety design: OpenAI’s Operator system card and Anthropic’s computer use announcement.
  • The column’s reading list (in Chinese, with English titles) lives in the repository at docs/reading-lists/3d-gui-agent.md.

Exercises

  1. Grounding error and target size. Using the formula of section 3.1, compute the hit probability for a 44 x 44 px button and for a 12 x 12 px icon at $\sigma = 4$, 8 and 15 px. Then estimate the $\sigma$ at which a model would score 50% on targets of 12 px. What does this suggest about the value of zooming in by a factor of 2?

    Hint

    For the 44 px button ($a = b = 22$): about 1.00, 0.99 and 0.74. For the 12 px icon ($a = b = 6$): 0.75, 0.30 and 0.09. A 50% hit rate needs $\operatorname{erf}(6/(\sigma\sqrt2)) = 0.707$, i.e. $6/(\sigma\sqrt2) \approx 0.74$, so $\sigma \approx 5.7$ px. Zooming by 2 doubles the target in pixels while the model’s error in pixels stays roughly the same, so a 12 px target behaves like a 24 px one, which is why ScreenSeekeR and zoom modes gain so much. You can check the numbers in the grounding mode of the widget.

  2. Choose an observation. You are building an agent for a hospital’s in-house Windows application whose custom-drawn widgets expose no UI Automation names. List the observation options of section 2, say which you would use and why, and say what data you would collect first.

    Hint

    Without names the tree gives boxes at best, so the screenshot must carry the semantics; a parser (OmniParser-style) or a native screenshot model is the primary input, with whatever structure exists as an extra signal. Collecting a small grounding set (screenshots with labelled target boxes for the application’s frequent operations) lets you measure grounding accuracy, the most likely bottleneck, before building anything else.

  3. Reliability arithmetic. An agent succeeds on a task with probability 0.85 per attempt. Compute pass@3 and pass^3. Then assume the task needs 40 steps and each step succeeds with probability $q$; what $q$ gives 85% task success without recovery? What does this say about where to invest: better steps or recovery?

    Hint

    pass@3 $= 1 - 0.15^3 = 0.997$; pass^3 $= 0.85^3 = 0.614$. From $q^{40} = 0.85$ you get $q = 0.85^{1/40} \approx 0.9959$, i.e. fewer than one failed step in 240. Pushing single-step accuracy that high is hard; detecting and undoing a failed step (reflection, section 4.3) relaxes the requirement, because a step only has to be right eventually.

  4. A reward for 3D grounding. Design a GRPO reward for a model that, given a rendered XR view and an instruction, outputs a pixel to cast a ray through. Use the engine’s colliders. How would you handle occluded targets and tiny distant targets, and how could the reward be hacked?

    Hint

    A natural reward is 1 if the first collider hit by the ray belongs to the target, plus a smooth term (like GUI-G²’s Gaussian reward) based on the angular distance between the ray and the target’s centre, scaled by the target’s angular size, so that small far targets are not hopeless. For occluded targets, decide whether the correct output is the occluder (to move it), a “change viewpoint” action, or the target through the occluder; reward the choice you want. Hacks: rays aimed at large objects that contain the target’s collider (e.g. a whole window instead of a button), so use the smallest interactable collider.

  5. Hands-on: the widget. In the photo episode, switch to the grounding mode on step 3 (the toolbar) and find the smallest $\sigma$ at which a point placed at the centre of the Share icon hits Share less than 90% of the time. Then do the same for the Wi-Fi row in the Settings screen. Explain the difference with the formula of section 3.1.

    Hint

    The Share icon’s touch box is 44 x 44 px, so the hit rate falls below 90% at about $\sigma \approx 11$ px; the Wi-Fi row is 328 x 52 px, so only the vertical direction matters and $\sigma$ must exceed about 16 px. The sampled percentages in the widget use 400 samples, so expect a few points of noise around the formula.

Next: Why 3D interfaces are hard to operate, the human side of the problem: what makes spatial UIs harder than screens, and which operations a 3D GUI agent should take over.
entry.summary: How AI agents operate phones, desktops and the web: the perceive-plan-ground-act loop, screenshots versus accessibility trees, grounding models from SeeClick to GroundCascade, planning, reflection and memory, training with synthetic data and reinforcement learning, benchmarks and the state of the art as of November 2026, humans in the loop, safety, and what carries over to 3D interfaces.

entry.title: 3D GUI agents: a research vision for operating the interfaces of VR, AR and MR for the user

link.title: 3D GUI agents: a research vision for operating the interfaces of VR, AR and MR for the user

entry.content:
Why this matters

Phones did not become everyday devices only because they are useful. They also became easy to operate: one flat screen in the hand, a tap on what you see, a keyboard on which people type about 36 words per minute on average. In the last three years a second change happened on top of that. GUI agents, AI models that read a screen and tap, type and scroll for a user, learned to operate phones, desktops and websites; on the desktop benchmark OSWorld they went from 12% of tasks in April 2024 to above the human baseline in December 2025 (post 2). A person can now say what they want and let an agent work through the interface.

Headsets and XR glasses have had neither moment. Their interfaces are spatial: windows float around the user, buttons sit at different depths, menus are opened with gestures that have to be learned, and text is typed in mid-air. Operating them is measurably slower, less accurate and more tiring than operating a phone (post 3). And we found no published evaluation of an agent that operates them for the user in the way phone agents do (post 4).

This column proposes to bring the two together: a 3D GUI agent that operates the spatial interface of a VR, AR or MR device for the user, or guides the user through it. This post states the idea, defines it, argues for it with the evidence collected in posts 2 to 4, says honestly what it can and cannot do, and lists the open questions. This post fixes the direction as of November 2026. It describes a research direction, not a result: we have no system and no numbers of our own to report yet.

Prerequisites

  • What a GUI agent is (observe, ground, act, verify; task success on a benchmark). Post 2 explains it from scratch.
  • Basic 3D interaction vocabulary (ray pointing, gaze and pinch, windows and volumes in space). Post 3 covers it with numbers.
  • Nothing else. This post is the entry point of the column and keeps the technical detail light; the three survey posts carry the depth.

1. What we mean by a 3D GUI agent

1.1 The definition

We call a 3D GUI agent an agent that takes a user’s request, in speech or text and optionally with pointing, perceives the spatial user interface of a VR, AR or MR device, and either operates that interface on the user’s behalf or guides the user through it.

Four parts of this sentence carry weight.

  1. The goal comes from the user, in language. “Open the browser”, “bring the music player here”, “turn on the setting that stops the boundary from showing”. Pointing, gaze and head direction can complete the sentence: “put that over there” only makes sense together with where the user is pointing. The goal is not inferred from coverage targets (as in automated testing) or from a game’s reward.
  2. The agent perceives the spatial user interface (spatial UI): windows, panels, volumes, menus and widgets placed around the user in 3D, seen through the rendered view and, where the platform allows it, through UI structure (a scene graph or an accessibility tree). It perceives the interface, not mainly the physical room.
  3. It acts in one of several ways. It can operate the interface itself (select, press, grab, move, resize, type, navigate menus and apps); it can guide the user (explain, highlight, coach); and it can ask when the request is ambiguous or the step is consequential. Section 6 treats these modes as a spectrum.
  4. It is judged by task success on interfaces it did not author. An agent that changes the virtual world through the engine of its own app is solving a different problem. The test of a 3D GUI agent is whether it completes users’ requests on the interfaces of existing apps and of the system, as phone agents are tested on apps they did not write.

We do not claim that the term or the idea has never been used. The arXiv title of Orienter (Shuqing Li et al., published at FSE 2026) already speaks of a “Vision-Based Spatial Intelligent Agent” for XR apps, and vendors already describe assistants that act on headsets (section 7). What this column contributes is a precise problem statement, a motivation, and a research program around it.

1.2 The loop, on a phone and on a headset

A phone GUI agent runs a loop: observe the screen, ground the next step on an element (“the Share button” becomes a location), act (tap, type, swipe), and verify that the screen changed as expected. A 3D GUI agent runs the same loop, but each box changes, as the figure shows.

1.3 What is in scope, and what is not

A useful definition says what it excludes. These are the boundaries we draw, each with its reason.

In scope:

  • 2D panels placed in 3D. Most of what people do on a headset happens in flat windows: a browser, a settings panel, a mail app, often 2D Android apps running unmodified as panels. Their content is a 2D GUI, but finding them, reaching them and arranging them is a 3D problem.
  • The spatial system UI. Launchers, quick settings, the window manager, the recentre and boundary controls, the system keyboard: the layer every user has to operate, and the one where buried settings live.
  • 3D widgets and volumes. Sliders and dials in space, 3D models to rotate or scale, volumetric apps whose controls are objects rather than buttons.
  • The UI of immersive apps, when the task is an interface operation. Changing a setting inside a VR app, opening its menu, selecting an item in its inventory screen. The line is the task, not the app: operating the app’s interface is in scope, playing the app is not.
  • Multi-app tasks. “Put the recipe next to the timer and start a 10-minute countdown” spans two apps and the window layer, like the cross-app tasks that recent 2D benchmarks such as MobileWorld include (post 2).

Out of scope:

  • Generating XR content (LLMs that build or edit scenes, such as LLMR at CHI 2024). The agent changes the world through the engine; it does not operate an interface made by someone else.
  • Guidance for physical tasks (assembling furniture, repairing a machine with AR instructions, as in Guided Reality at UIST 2025). The object of the task is the real world, not the GUI, although its visual vocabulary of arrows and highlights is useful for our guide mode.
  • Answering questions about the view (GazePointAR at CHI 2024, glasses assistants). Answering is perception and dialogue without action; it is a component, not the goal.
  • Automated testing (VRExplorer, XRintTest, Meta XR Operator used by coding agents). These systems drive VR apps very effectively, but their goal is coverage of all interactions, not one user’s request; we reuse their machinery, not their problem.
  • Gameplay. Playing for the user removes the reason the user is there; a study of AI companions in VR games found that autonomous agent play lowered workload but hurt challenge, autonomy, immersion and enjoyment (Taiyu Zhang et al., arXiv 2609.13727, 2026).
  • Display-free glasses (camera-and-audio AI glasses). They have no spatial GUI to operate; their assistants act through services and APIs. Glasses with a display, and XR glasses that show windows, are in scope.

2. Why 3D interfaces are hard to operate

Post 3 collects the evidence in detail. The short version:

Operating a 3D interface has measured costs that a phone does not have: slower and less accurate pointing in depth, mid-air text entry at roughly half of phone typing speed, arm fatigue, and novices who do not know which action to take.

Each cost has a source:

  • Pointing in depth. On a stereo display, virtual-hand movements along the viewing direction were about 25% slower than lateral ones, with about 20% lower throughput, well beyond what the change in visual size explains (Barrera Machuca and Stuerzlinger, CHI 2019). With gaze and pinch on a Quest Pro, selection also slows down with depth (Bashar et al., arXiv 2607.27369, to appear in IEEE TVCG / ISMAR 2026).
  • Selection errors. In a field study in a car (Varjo XR-3, N = 24), 8.8 to 23.5% of selections failed with the car standing still and 20.4 to 36.0% while it was moving, depending on the technique (Sasalovici et al., CHI 2025). With ray selection at 8 m on a Quest 3, 15.2% of selections failed with a controller and 32.9% with a bare hand, mostly because the confirm action itself moved the ray (Qiu et al., arXiv 2602.01061, accepted to IEEE TVCG / IEEE VR 2026 according to the authors). On a phone, 37,370 people typing left 2.3% of errors uncorrected (Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019).
  • Text entry. Phone typing averaged 36.2 words per minute (wpm) in the same study. On a virtual keyboard in VR, the fastest of six selection methods, pointing with a controller, reached 15.44 wpm (Speicher et al., CHI 2018), and the mean over 137 XR text-entry techniques with a reported speed is 20.36 wpm (Bhatia et al., CHI 2025): roughly half of phone speed, or less.
  • Arm fatigue. Mid-air input holds the arm against gravity; Consumed Endurance (Hincapié-Ramos et al., CHI 2014) made this “gorilla-arm” cost measurable and showed that it appears even when time and errors do not differ. Bare-hand ray selection puts the hand 14.3% higher and 66.2% further forward than a controller (Luong et al., IEEE TVCG 2023), and Apple’s guidelines call direct gestures “best for infrequent use”.
  • Not knowing what to do. Observing 25 novices with four consumer AR apps, Khurana et al. (IMWUT 2023) found that most errors occurred when participants could not determine the correct sequence of actions or could not evaluate what their action had done. These are failures of knowledge, not of motor control, and an agent that knows the interface addresses exactly them.

The figure puts the main numbers side by side.

Two further costs come from the space itself. Content can be anywhere. A window can be behind the user, hidden behind another window, or left in another room, and the user has to turn around or recentre to find it; the platforms leave this to the user’s head and hands (post 3, section 3.4). And the view changes with every head movement, which matters as much for an agent that sees what the user sees as for the user. The next figure, and the widget in section 5, make this concrete.

3. Does this matter for everyday XR? An honest answer

This column starts from an intuition: that the complexity of operating 3D interfaces is one reason why 3D mobile terminals have not entered everyday life. That is a hypothesis, and the evidence supports it only partly. We state the position we can defend:

The difficulty of operating 3D interfaces is one of several barriers to everyday XR, alongside, and usually behind, price, comfort, content and motion sickness. An agent can lower the operating cost; it cannot fix weight, price or sickness.

The evidence behind “usually behind” is clear (post 3, section 5). Among US adults who were not buying a Vision Pro in February 2024 (Variety VIP+ with CivicScience, N = 1,069), 65.5% named the price, 15% discomfort, 13.5% nausea and 12.2% the lack of content. In 3,205 Amazon reviews of ten VR devices, discomfort accounted for 39% of the coded themes, health risk for 30%, missing content for 21%, and ease of use for 7% (Dehghani et al., 2021). Owners who stop using headsets cite comfort and health more than operation.

The evidence for “one of several barriers” is also real, and it points at the parts of operation an agent can address:

  • Discoverability. In the same Vision Pro survey, 22.3% said they were not aware of what the device could do. Some owners filmed in everyday use did not know that Travel Mode existed (Tran et al., CHI 2025), and analysts testing the Vision Pro described a learning curve with eyes, hands and gestures.
  • Learning. The novice errors of Khurana et al. are about not knowing the sequence, the gulf of execution, which is the step a GUI agent takes over on a phone.
  • Ease of use in acceptance models. Ease of use and cognitive affordance appear as significant antecedents of AR and VR acceptance in survey models, next to usefulness, comfort and social norms (post 3, section 5.3).

And there is counter-evidence: early adopters describe the Vision Pro interface as intuitive, and the fastest-growing device class, AI glasses, has almost no GUI at all, which can be read as “simpler interaction wins” or as “cheaper and lighter wins”. No survey we found even offered “too hard to use” as an answer. The missing evidence is part of the research: if a 3D GUI agent works, it becomes possible to measure how much operating cost matters, by removing it.

So we do not claim that agents will bring headsets into daily life. We claim something narrower: the cost of operating a 3D interface is real and measured, it appears in the adoption evidence as one barrier among several, it is a barrier that software can lower directly, and lowering it is worth studying for its own sake and for the users in the next section.

4. The strongest case: accessibility

Accessibility is the strongest near-term case: screen readers in XR can describe and enumerate, but users still fail to operate menus; with AI scene description, blind and low-vision participants completed 11% of VR menu trials.

The platforms already ship assistive services that read a UI tree and act for the user: VoiceOver, Pointer Control and Voice Control on Vision Pro, TalkBack on Android XR, a screen reader in the experimental settings of Meta Quest. They work for the system UI and for 2D panels with labels. They cannot act on unlabelled 3D content, which is most of what immersive apps draw, they do not convey spatial structure (what is left, behind, near), and they cannot turn a free-form 3D manipulation into a command (post 3, section 6). Voice Control on Vision Pro can reach any labelled element, but the user has to name every step.

VRSight (Killough et al., UIST 2025) is the clearest measurement of what is left. It describes unmodified VR apps from the headset video, using a detector trained on 17,691 VR images, depth estimation, OCR and GPT-4o, in about 2.3 to 2.6 s per query. Nine blind and low-vision participants used it in Rec Room. All of them found the menu, but only one found the specific button the task asked for: menu trials had an 11% completion rate. Participants asked for d-pad navigation, snapping and row-by-row reading, in other words for a discrete action space. For low-vision users, the SeeingVR toolkit (Zhao et al., CHI 2019) raised the number of participants who completed a menu task from 4 of 11 to 11 of 11, but it needs tools built into each app or applied post hoc.

Describing a scene is far easier than operating a 3D UI, and the step that fails is exactly the step an operating agent would take. The case is also immediate: a blind user cannot wait for headsets to become cheaper or lighter before the menu works. Two cautions from the 2D literature apply. GUI agents are themselves often inaccessible: a computer-use agent that succeeded on 78.3% of tasks dropped to 28.3% with a screen magnifier (A11y-CUA, CHI 2026). And agents that act silently make choices the user cannot see: in the formative study of Morae (Peng et al., UIST 2025), an agent reported “completed” for 484 of 576 feasible requests in a study with blind and low-vision users, but only 189 were correct. For accessibility, a 3D GUI agent must ask at decision points and report what it did.

5. From phone agents to 3D GUI agents: what transfers and what breaks

Post 2 surveys the 2D field and ends with a careful list of what carries over. Our summary:

Much of the phone GUI-agent recipe transfers (screenshots plus structure, element-level actions, execution-based evaluation); what breaks is that the agent’s view changes with every head movement, targets can be small, distant, occluded or behind the user, actions are 3D, and the user waits inside the interface.

What transfers. Three lessons from 2D are strong enough to adopt from the start:

  • Screenshots plus structure. Screenshot-first models cover every app, and accessibility trees or the DOM help where they exist. XR has the same two sources: the rendered view, and the scene graph or the platform’s spatial semantics (Android XR’s subspace semantics tree, RealityKit’s AccessibilityComponent), although on most platforms only the app itself, its tests or the system can read this structure today.
  • Element-level actions. The choice of action space matters as much as the model: with GPT-4 held fixed, AppAgent’s success rose from 2.2% with raw coordinate actions to 48.9% with actions over numbered elements (C. Zhang et al., CHI 2025). An XR agent should likewise act on targets (a window, a button, a slider) through a small set of verbs, and leave the rays and pinches to a low-level controller.
  • Execution-based evaluation. AndroidWorld (Rawles et al., ICLR 2025) and OSWorld (Xie et al., NeurIPS 2024) run the agent in a real environment and check the final state with a program. That is the only kind of evaluation that measures whether a user’s request was actually carried out.

What breaks. Four assumptions of 2D agents fail in a headset:

  1. The view changes with every head movement. A phone screenshot shows the whole interface and stays the same until something is tapped. A headset frame shows only the part of the interface in the field of view, and a different part a moment later. One UI state produces endless different images.
  2. Targets can be small, distant, occluded or behind the user. A 2 cm button on a panel 1.5 m away covers less than 1° of visual angle; a window can hide another; the window the user asks for may be behind them. The agent must decide where to look, or ask the user to turn, and it needs a memory of where things are.
  3. Actions are 3D. Rays, pinches, grabs, two-handed scaling, 6-DoF poses, gaze, locomotion. The best of seven language models tested on ComboBench (Gemini 1.5 Pro, with five examples in the prompt) produced the exact controller sequence for a VR action in 11.7% of its 262 scenarios, and none exceeded 5.8% without examples (Shuqing Li et al., arXiv 2510.24706, 2025).
  4. The user waits inside the interface. On a desktop an agent can work in the background for twenty minutes. In a headset the user watches, the world keeps rendering at 90 frames per second, and the content may move while the agent thinks. The XR agent prototypes compared in post 4 take about 4 s (DuoZone) to about 49 s (NavAI) per turn; a delay above about 4 s already degrades the experience with LLM-driven agents in VR (Maslych et al., CUI 2025).

The interactive sketch below lets you feel the first two points. Turn the head and watch what an agent that sees through the user’s eyes can and cannot know.

Where is the UI? A top-down room with five floating windows around the user (purple dot). Drag or swipe sideways to turn the head; the wedge is the field of view in one frame, and the strip below it is what the agent sees in that frame. Windows are marked as in view, at the edge of the view, occluded by a nearer window, outside the view, or behind the user. Switch on ‘memory’ to keep faded markers of windows seen before, press ‘rearrange’ to move windows while you are not looking, and pick a request to see whether the agent could act from the current view or must first turn, search or recall. The layout is illustrative and encodes no benchmark parameters.

6. Do it, show me, or ask me: the autonomy spectrum

On a phone, a GUI agent is usually expected to do the whole task. In a headset, the user is present, embodied and often there for the experience. We therefore take the position that:

A 3D GUI agent should not always take over: some operations are better done for the user, some better shown, and sometimes the agent should ask.

We distinguish six points on a spectrum from explaining to acting, with an example operation for each:

Mode What the agent does Example operation
Explain says in words how to do it “How do I turn on Travel Mode?”
Show where highlights the target in space, or draws a ray hint to it find the recentre control in the quick settings
Coach leads step by step, waits for the user to act, confirms each step learn the pinch-and-drag gesture that moves a window
Reshape the layout moves, enlarges or brings content closer so the user can act easily bring the music player from behind the user to the front; enlarge a distant panel for a low-vision user
Propose and act previews a change and applies it after the user confirms arrange three windows for writing a report
Act with takeover carries out the steps while the user watches and can interrupt type a search query; change a buried setting

At every point the agent can also ask: which window was meant by “that”, whether to overwrite, whether to continue after an unexpected dialog.

The published evidence that the choice matters comes from three directions:

  • DuoZone (Qian et al., IEEE TVCG 2026), an LLM-guided window manager on Vision Pro, proposes layouts and applies them only after the user confirms. With 16 professionals it made layout matching 34.5% faster and building a workspace took 168.3 s instead of 218.1 s, yet participants accepted 90.3% of app recommendations, 82.8% of sizing and 76.5% of ordering decisions: users changed up to about a quarter of the decisions. Propose-and-act fits a task where the user has preferences.
  • VRCopilot (L. Zhang et al., UIST 2024) compared manual, fully automatic and scaffolded co-creation of VR layouts; fully automatic creation gave users a lower sense of agency than scaffolding, where the AI proposes a wireframe and the user edits it.
  • The study of AI companions in VR games (Taiyu Zhang et al., arXiv 2609.13727, preprint, 2026; N = 24 on Vision Pro) compared no help, command-based help, discussion and autonomous agent play. Autonomous play gave the lowest workload, but lowered challenge, autonomy, immersion and enjoyment.

The 2D literature adds that users prefer to confirm at intermediate steps rather than only at the end (81% of 48 participants in “When Should Users Check?”, CHI 2026), and the XR guidance systems of post 4 (Sensible Agent, Guided Reality, AgentHands) give a vocabulary for the show-and-coach end. What is missing is evidence for GUI operation in XR: which operations users want done, which shown, and when they want to be asked. We do not propose a rule here; how to choose the mode is one of the open questions of section 8.

7. What exists already

Post 4 maps the closest work in depth, with a rubric and a heat map of 23 works and products. The picture it draws:

Pieces of such an agent already exist: detection of GUI elements in VR frames, LLM window management from speech and pointing, LLM navigation from VR screenshots, and tools that let agents drive VR apps for testing.

  • Detection of GUI elements in VR frames. Orienter (Shuqing Li et al., FSE 2026) finds interactable elements in screenshots of 100 Steam VR apps with a large multimodal model plus an open-vocabulary detector, reaching an interactability F1 of 44.10% at IoU 0.75, against 2.21% for the 2D screen parser OmniParser. VRSight’s DISCOVR dataset (UIST 2025) labels menus, buttons and UI text in 17,691 frames from 17 VR apps, mostly social VR.
  • LLM window management from speech and pointing. Revisiting Put-That-There (Bovo et al., ISMAR 2025 Adjunct) turns speech, pointing and head direction into JSON actions that place or remove windows on the surfaces of the room, without a user study yet; DuoZone (section 6) does window layout with confirmation and a 16-person evaluation.
  • LLM navigation from VR screenshots. NavAI (Qin and DiGiovanni, ASE 2025 Workshops) closes the loop from a language goal and field-of-view screenshots to executed movement in Unity scenes, completing 16 of 18 goal tasks at about 49 s per turn; it moves the viewpoint and does not touch menus.
  • Tools that let agents drive VR apps for testing. Meta XR Operator (August 2026, experimental) lets a coding agent take screenshots of a running VR app and press buttons and work through menus; GenXR-Bench (Huang et al., arXiv 2610.29014, 2026) uses VLM actors to operate the XR apps that coding agents generate; VRExplorer and XRintTest drive Unity VR scenes for test coverage.

Close to these, SIAgent (Wang, Gu and Lu, IEEE TVCG 2026) has an agent execute VR operations from inferred eye-hand intent, without language, and GazePointAR resolves “this” and “that” from gaze and pointing to answer questions.

Vendors are moving in this direction: Google says Gemini on Galaxy XR can take actions across apps and organize windows; Apple’s Siri on visionOS 27 takes actions through app intents; Meta ships an experimental tool that lets coding agents drive VR apps. Their mechanisms and success rates are mostly undisclosed or limited to developer testing.

Google’s launch post for Galaxy XR (October 2025) says that Gemini can “take action on your behalf across your apps” and that “Hey Google, organize these windows” arranges open windows; no mechanism or evaluation is published. Apple’s Siri on visionOS 27 gets things done across apps through the actions that apps declare with App Intents; in its WWDC26 App Intents session Apple explains that Siri’s understanding of on-screen text is “limited to exactly what’s in the pixels”, so it cannot act on items that an app does not expose. Meta’s XR Operator is a developer tool that, in Meta’s words, “operates too slowly for real-time interaction”. These are strong signals that the direction is timely, and they also show the two routes: semantic actions that apps opt into, and operation of the GUI itself.

The capability heat map of post 4 (its section 2) rates 23 such works and products on four properties: perceiving the 3D UI, understanding a natural-language intent, operating the UI, and being evaluated. Every property is covered fully by some work; no row covers all four. Put together:

As of November 2026 we found no published work that evaluates an agent carrying out users’ natural-language requests by operating the 3D GUIs of XR apps, and no benchmark or dataset of such instruction-to-action tasks.

This statement rests on the searches behind posts 2 to 4 (arXiv, OpenAlex, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, proceedings and product pages, through 24 November 2026). Absence in a search is not proof of absence, and the gap is narrow: Orienter perceives, Put-That-There and DuoZone act on the window layer from language, NavAI closes a loop, Meta XR Operator gives agents hands, and Gemini on Galaxy XR claims cross-app actions. The idea is therefore timely and partly anticipated. What it adds is the combination: one agent, driven by a user’s request, operating general 3D GUIs of existing apps, evaluated by task success, with the spatial problems of section 5 treated as the core of the research rather than as details.

8. Open questions

We keep these at the level of questions. Each is large enough for several studies.

  1. How should a 3D GUI agent be measured? 2D agents are evaluated by task success in resettable environments with programmatic checks. A 3D version needs tasks that real users would ask for, success checks that tolerate spatial variation (a window placed “next to” another), viewpoint variation, and human baselines (time, errors, effort) for the same tasks, which do not exist for whole tasks on commercial headsets either.
  2. How should an agent see an interface that changes with every head movement? Through the user’s eyes, through its own rendered views, through the scene graph or accessibility structure, or through a combination; and how should it remember where windows are when they leave the view, or move while nobody looks?
  3. Which actions should it use? Device-level input (rays, pinches, poses) works on every app but is slow and fragile; semantic actions (app intents, function calls) are reliable but cover only apps that opt in. What the right level is, and how to fall back between them, is open in XR.
  4. When should it do, guide or ask? Section 6 shows that the choice matters and that full autonomy is not always wanted. Which signals (the user’s goal, expertise, the reversibility of the action, whether the user is there to enjoy the experience) should decide it, and how the user stays in control, are not known for GUI operation in XR.
  5. Does it make XR accessible? Whether a 3D GUI agent can turn VRSight’s 11% into routine success for blind users, help users with limited mobility reach content behind them, and help older adults past the first sessions, has to be shown with those users, not assumed.

Beneath all five lie the platform questions of post 4: third-party apps are closed on devices, gaze stays private, and the most open environments (WebXR, emulators, simulators) are not the ones people use every day. Safety and privacy run through all of them: an agent that sees what the user sees, in the user’s home, must not become a channel for deceptive UI, prompt injection from the room, or the leakage of biometric traces.

9. What this column does next

We are building an open benchmark and a first prototype on Meta Quest, and will report results when they exist.

The rest of the column is the evidence base for that work:

  • Post 2: GUI agents on 2D screens, a survey of phone, desktop and web agents up to November 2026, ending with what transfers to 3D and what breaks.
  • Post 3: why 3D interfaces are hard to operate, the evidence on input, spatial UI structure, measured difficulty, adoption and accessibility, with a catalogue of 30 headset operations.
  • Post 4: AI agents in XR, the platforms and the gap, the closest work in depth, what each platform lets an agent observe and control, and the datasets.
  • The research plan, password-protected for now.

Representative papers

Status as of November 2026. “arXiv” means preprint only.

Paper Authors Venue Year Link Why it matters
3D User Interfaces: Theory and Practice (2nd ed.) J. J. LaViola Jr., E. Kruijff, R. P. McMahan, D. A. Bowman, I. Poupyrev Book, Addison-Wesley 2017 publisher The standard taxonomy of 3D interaction tasks (selection, manipulation, travel, system control)
AppAgent: Multimodal Agents as Smartphone Users C. Zhang et al. CHI 2025 arXiv Element-level actions and exploration documents for phone agents
AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents C. Rawles et al. ICLR 2025 arXiv Parameterized tasks with programmatic success checks
OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments T. Xie et al. NeurIPS (D&B) 2024 arXiv Execution-based evaluation on real desktops; the curve that measured progress
Look Before You Leap: Context-Sensitive GUI Grounding for Boosting Automated Extended Reality (XR) Testing (Orienter) S. Li et al. FSE (PACMSE) 2026 DOI Grounding of interactable GUI elements in rendered VR frames
DuoZone: A User-Centric, LLM-Guided Mixed-Initiative XR Window Management System J. Qian et al. IEEE TVCG 2026 arXiv Language-driven window layout with confirmation, evaluated with 16 users
Revisiting put-that-there, context aware window interactions via LLMs R. Bovo et al. ISMAR Adjunct 2025 arXiv LLM actions on XR windows from speech, pointing and head direction
NavAI: A Generalizable LLM Framework for Navigation Tasks in Virtual Reality Environments X. Qin, M. DiGiovanni ASE Workshops 2025 arXiv Closed loop from language and VR screenshots to movement
SIAgent: Spatial Interaction Agent via LLM-powered Eye-Hand Motion Intent Understanding in VR Z. Wang, C. Gu, F. Lu IEEE TVCG 2026 arXiv An agent executes VR operations from inferred intent
VRSight: An AI-Driven Scene Description System to Improve Virtual Reality Accessibility for Blind People D. Killough et al. UIST 2025 DOI 11% menu completion with scene description: describing is not operating
GazePointAR: A Context-Aware Multimodal Voice Assistant for Pronoun Disambiguation in Wearable Augmented Reality J. Lee et al. CHI 2024 arXiv Deictic requests resolved from gaze and pointing
Guided Reality: Generating Visually-Enriched AR Task Guidance with LLMs and Vision Models A. Y. Zhao et al. UIST 2025 arXiv A visual vocabulary for spatial guidance
VRCopilot: Authoring 3D Layouts with Generative AI Models in VR L. Zhang et al. UIST 2024 DOI Full automation lowers the sense of agency
“What Can I Do for You”: How Should AI Companions Provide Assistance to Players in Virtual Reality Games T. Zhang et al. arXiv 2026 arXiv Autonomous agent play lowers workload but also enjoyment
“Do I Just Tap My Headset?”: How Novice Users Discover Gestural Interactions with Consumer Augmented Reality Applications A. Khurana et al. IMWUT 2023 DOI Most novice errors: not knowing what to do or what happened, rather than moving
Selection-based Text Entry in Virtual Reality M. Speicher et al. CHI 2018 DOI VR keyboards at 5.3 to 15.4 wpm
Bumpy Ride? Understanding the Effects of External Forces on Spatial Interactions in Moving Vehicles M. Sasalovici et al. CHI 2025 DOI Selection error rates on a current headset, still and moving

Product sources: Introducing Galaxy XR (Google, October 2025); Introducing Meta XR Operator (Meta, 18 August 2026); Apple introduces Siri AI (Apple, 8 June 2026), Explore advanced App Intents features for Siri and Apple Intelligence (WWDC26 session 343) and About visionOS 27 updates (Apple).

Learning resources

  • The column’s research dossiers in the repository, docs/research/3d-gui-agent/: GUI agents in 2D, 3D UI and XR interaction, agents in XR and 3D, and platforms and tooling, each with verified citations. The reading list is docs/reading-lists/3d-gui-agent.md.
  • The 3D UI book above (LaViola et al., 2017) for the interaction vocabulary, and Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines for spatial design for how one platform turns it into rules.
  • For hands-on agent work: AndroidWorld and OSWorld for environments and checkers; Meta’s IWER for a scriptable WebXR headset in the browser.
  • The W3C XR Accessibility User Requirements, which describe what an accessible XR interface must allow; they read like the preconditions of a 3D GUI agent.

Exercises

  1. Time a buried setting. On a headset you have access to, change one setting that takes several steps (for example, the passthrough or boundary behaviour, or the keyboard language). Time it, count the steps, and note every moment you did not know what to do next. Then do the same setting on a phone, if it has an equivalent.

    Hint

    Separate three kinds of cost while you time: knowing where the setting is (knowledge), reaching and selecting each control (motor), and checking that it took effect (evaluation). Khurana et al. found most novice errors in the first and third; an agent helps most there.

  2. Delegate or not. For the task of exercise 1, mark each step as “do it for me”, “show me where”, or “I want to do it myself”. Which steps did you delegate, and why?

    Hint

    Steps that are pure navigation (opening menus, scrolling) are good candidates to delegate; the final decision (which value) often is not, because it carries your preference. This is the propose-and-act pattern of DuoZone: the agent prepares, you confirm.

  3. Never for me. Describe one operation on a headset that an agent should never do for you, and one it should only do after asking. What property of the operation decides it?

    Hint

    Consider reversibility (deleting, sending, paying), safety (changing the boundary or passthrough hides the real room), secrets (passwords), and experiences you are there to have (playing a game). Post 3’s catalogue of 30 operations marks several as “neither”.

  4. Turn and remember. In the widget of section 5, choose the request “bring the music player here” with memory off and turn until the agent could act. Then switch memory on, look around once, turn back, and press “rearrange”. What does the agent believe now, and what should it do before acting?

    Hint

    With memory on, the agent remembers where it last saw each window, which saves a search, until something moves. After “rearrange” its memory is stale: a careful agent treats remembered positions as hints and verifies before acting, the way a 2D agent re-reads the screen after every action.

  5. What transfers. Pick one 2D GUI-agent technique from post 2 (for example Set-of-Mark labels, exploration documents, or reflection) and describe in a paragraph what it would look like in a headset, and which of the four broken assumptions of section 5 it would have to deal with.

    Hint

    Set-of-Mark labels, for example, become marks attached to objects in space; they must stay attached when the head moves (assumption 1), they cannot label what is behind the user (assumption 2), and a label on a tiny distant button is still hard to hit with a ray (assumption 3).

Next: Post 2: GUI agents on 2D screens.
entry.summary: Why the 3D interfaces of headsets and XR glasses are hard to operate, and the research direction this column proposes: agents that operate the spatial GUI on the user's behalf, or guide the user through it.

entry.title: Paper Digest | October-November 2026: graphics, engines, neural rendering, world models, embodied AI and XR

link.title: Paper Digest | October-November 2026: graphics, engines, neural rendering, world models, embodied AI and XR

entry.content:
About this issue

This is the first issue of the Paper Digest, a dated column that sits next to the learning series of this blog. The learning series (graphics, neural rendering, graphics engines, world models, embodied AI) explain the foundations. The digest shows what researchers did with those foundations last month.

Window and date stamp. This issue covers papers whose first version appeared between 1 October and 2 November 2026. It was compiled on 2 November 2026, and every status below is “as of” that date. When a paper is accepted later, the status here will be out of date.

How the papers were chosen. I swept the arXiv listings of cs.GR, cs.CV, cs.RO, cs.HC, cs.LG and cs.AI for the window, ran keyword queries (Gaussian splatting, world model, vision-language-action, humanoid, virtual reality, path tracing, neural shading and others), and read the arXiv comments for acceptances at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026, NeurIPS 2026, CoRL 2026, UIST 2026, ISMAR 2026 and IEEE TVCG. From a few hundred candidates I kept 42 papers, 7 per category, preferring, in order:

  1. significance: a new capability or a clearly stronger result;
  2. acceptance at a top venue;
  3. open code or data;
  4. relevance to graphics, 3D vision, AR/VR, HCI, world models and embodied AI.

What was verified. For every entry I opened the arXiv abstract page and checked the title, first author, first-submission date and the comments field; project and code links were opened once. Affiliations are given only when the paper’s own pages state them. Numbers are quoted only as “the authors report …”. The summaries are mine: they are written from the abstracts and project pages, not copied, and a short summary cannot replace reading the paper.

Status labels. “SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (accepted)” and similar labels come from the arXiv comments field. “Preprint” means that no venue was stated, not that the paper was rejected. A preprint has not been peer reviewed.

How to read an entry. Each entry has four parts: what it does, how it works (the key idea, at the level of a graduate student), what is new compared with prior work, and the connection to CG: which representation, rendering, geometry, simulation, animation or interaction idea it uses or changes, with links to the chapters of this blog that explain the background.

Explore this issue

The explorer below contains all 42 entries. Filter by category or by connection to computer graphics, scrub along the timeline, and tap a paper to read its summary and open its links.

Interactive explorer. Tap a category chip to show only that category (tap more chips to add categories, or All to reset). Tap a CG link such as rendering to keep only papers that touch it. Tap or drag across the dots to select a paper; the card shows its summary from this page, with links to the paper, code, project page and the full entry.

1. Graphics

Rendering, geometry, physical simulation, animation and imaging. This month the graphics papers are mostly about simulation: differentiable contact, learned integrators, material point methods and Monte Carlo PDE solvers. Background: physically based simulation and animation and characters.

1. Tabula Rasa: Monte Carlo estimation of unit-variance noise with controlled spatio-temporal correlation

Tobias Ritschel et al. (7 authors) · SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers (accepted) · first submitted 8 Oct 2026 · code

  • What it does. It generates noise fields that have exactly unit variance and a chosen correlation over space and time. Rendering and simulation pipelines use such fields for dithering, sampling and procedural detail.
  • How it works. The authors treat noise synthesis as a Monte Carlo estimation problem: they estimate a pixel reconstruction and its variance together, and normalize by the variance estimate. To do so cheaply they borrow sketching, a technique from database research that summarizes large data streams in small, fixed-size structures.
  • What is new. Earlier ways to build correlated noise with controlled temporal coherence are more complex. The authors report that their generator is simpler and faster than earlier methods.
  • Connection to CG. Noise with a controlled spectrum decides how Monte Carlo error looks in a frame and how it flickers over time, which in turn decides how well a temporal denoiser can remove it. See Monte Carlo estimation in ray and path tracing and the temporal reuse in real-time ray tracing.

2. DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU

Kemeng Huang et al. (5 authors, with Taku Komura) · preprint · first submitted 13 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It is a GPU simulator for Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) that you can differentiate. It handles scenes that mix soft deformable bodies with nearly rigid ones.
  • How it works. Nearly rigid parts are modeled as affine bodies: each has only 12 degrees of freedom, a 3x3 matrix and a translation. Soft parts use full finite-element (FEM) coordinates. For the backward pass the method solves one coupled FEM-affine adjoint linear system per frame, so the system is much smaller, while the contact and friction terms stay coupled. A PyTorch interface connects user parameters and losses to the simulator.
  • What is new. Penalty-based or velocity-level differentiable simulators let objects interpenetrate or drift. IPC guarantees that they never intersect, but differentiating it was expensive. The authors report peak speedups over DiffIPC of about 150x with full-space FEM and about 4133x with affine bodies.
  • Connection to CG. IPC’s barrier energy keeps contacts free of intersections. Gradients through it enable inverse design, such as material and shape fitting, and system identification for robots. See implicit integration and contact in physically based simulation and the inverse problems in differentiable rendering.

3. Neuroll: Real-Time Neural Strand-Based Hair Simulation via Simulator-in-the-Loop Unrolling

Gene Wei-Chin Lin et al. · preprint · first submitted 3 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It is a neural time integrator for strand-based hair that runs in real time on commodity hardware.
  • How it works. The network takes the inputs a classical integrator would take: the previous hair states, the material stiffness and the collision geometry. It works in each strand’s local frame, so it does not depend on hair density. Training is self-supervised with the simulator in the loop: the network is unrolled over randomly chosen horizons, and the physics is enforced along the whole rollout, not just for one step.
  • What is new. Earlier neural hair and cloth simulators often lose physical plausibility and fail on inputs unlike their training data. This one aims at stable long rollouts that transfer across hairstyles, materials and body motions. It also supports quasi-static simulation by resetting the state.
  • Connection to CG. It is a learned replacement for the time-stepping loop in physically based simulation. It matters for real-time characters (animation and characters), where hair is among the most expensive secondary motions.

4. PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning

Yuanhang Lei et al. (12 authors) · preprint · first submitted 19 Oct 2026 · project

  • What it does. Given any static shape, a feed-forward network predicts a neural skinning field. The field defines a small deformation subspace in which elastic simulation runs in real time, with no per-object training.
  • How it works. A neural skinning field assigns each point a weight per handle, as in linear blend skinning. The handles’ affine transforms then become the reduced coordinates of the simulation. The autoencoder is trained self-supervised from physical energies, not simulation data. Normalized skinning fields and a conflict-aware gradient correction keep the physics loss and the orthogonality loss from fighting each other. Because the subspace is a field, it can drive meshes, point clouds and 3D Gaussians alike.
  • What is new. Earlier neural subspace methods, including the original PhysSkin, optimize one subspace per shape. PhysSkin++ predicts the subspace for unseen shapes.
  • Connection to CG. Skinning is the deformation model of animation and characters, and reduced-order elasticity is a classic speed-up in physically based simulation. Driving 3D Gaussians directly makes captured scenes physically animatable.

5. Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations

Timna Böttcher et al. (3 authors, with Jan Bender) · preprint · first submitted 27 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It is a material point method (MPM) for perfectly elastic solids that does not fracture artificially under large deformations and handles collisions naturally.
  • How it works. Standard MPM updates each particle’s deformation gradient $F$ from the grid velocity gradient. Errors accumulate in that update, and they show up as numerical fracture. Here, $F$ is derived directly from the particle positions relative to a fixed reference grid (“total” deformation), with no velocity-gradient update, and elastic forces are computed on the current, deformed grid.
  • What is new. Earlier total-Lagrangian MPM variants evaluate forces in the reference state, which makes standard collision handling awkward. This formulation supports collisions at the particle level and suppresses zero-energy modes.
  • Connection to CG. MPM is the workhorse for snow, sand and soft solids in film. See MPM and hyperelasticity in physically based simulation.

6. Walk on Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable and Composable Transport Medium Prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE Solvers

Yunfeng Liao et al. (2 authors) · preprint · first submitted 24 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It precompiles fine-scale transport inside heterogeneous materials into reusable, editable “prefabs” that Monte Carlo PDE solvers can plug in, so material edits become interactive.
  • How it works. Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves PDEs such as diffusion with random walks that jump between spheres, the same way a path tracer walks between surfaces, with no mesh. Inside a finely structured medium, walks become very short and slow. Each prefab stores coarse transition probabilities derived from multiscale finite-element bases, port-to-port operators, exit distributions and recorded trajectories. A hybrid WoS solver then jumps across a whole prefab in one step. The method also supports overlapping absorption fields, gradient steering through path reweighting, and transient diffusion.
  • What is new. Plain WoS and Walk-on-Stars must re-solve the fine scale after every edit. Prefabs make the medium composable, like instancing in a scene graph.
  • Connection to CG. Walk-based PDE solvers come from the rendering community and reuse its tools: importance sampling, path reweighting and BVH-style queries. Compare random walks in ray and path tracing and in volumes and participating media.

7. Dynamic Skinning: Kinematics-Driven Cartoon Effects for Articulated Characters

Damien Rohmer et al. (4 authors) · IEEE TVCG 2026 (accepted version) · first submitted 29 Oct 2026 · project

  • What it does. It adds physics-like secondary motion, such as jiggle, oscillation and waves running along a limb, to skinned characters without running a simulation.
  • How it works. A set of deformers offsets each vertex as a closed-form function of time and of the time derivatives of its position. The derivatives come from the skeleton’s motion, on top of standard skinning such as linear blend skinning (LBS). Because nothing is integrated over time, the result is fast, stable and directly controllable by artists.
  • What is new. It is a kinematic, closed-form alternative to simulation-based secondary motion: it gives cartoon-style effects at almost no cost and with no tuning of solver stability.
  • Connection to CG. It extends the skinning pipeline of animation and characters. Compare it with PhysSkin++ (entry 4): one uses real physics in a learned subspace, the other gets a physics-like look from kinematics alone.

2. Graphics engines and real-time

Real-time rendering, GPU and engine systems, neural shading in engines and tools. The common thread this month is moving expensive integration out of the frame: into a pre-integrated network (entry 10), a radiance cache (12), a hardware unit (13) or a hierarchy (14). Background: real-time ray tracing, real-time rendering techniques and GPU APIs and render graphs.

8. Windfoil: Closed-Form Coverage for Real-Time and Differentiable Vector Graphics

Matt DesLauriers (single author) · preprint · first submitted 1 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It is one WebGPU method that covers real-time vector-graphics rendering, high-resolution print rasterization and differentiable vector-graphics optimization.
  • How it works. A pixel’s coverage of a filled shape is the integral of the shape’s winding number over the pixel footprint. For contours made of quadratic Bézier curves, the paper evaluates this box-filtered winding number in closed form on the GPU. This gives anti-aliased coverage that is exact for a box filter, and the same formula is differentiable with respect to the control points.
  • What is new. It is compared with Skia and Slug for rendering and with DiffVG and Bézier Splatting for optimization. The author reports coverage closer to the reference at speeds comparable to Slug, and a fraction of the per-step cost when optimizing.
  • Connection to CG. This is anti-aliasing as integration over a pixel, the idea behind rasterization, applied to curves. Because the result is analytic and differentiable, it links to differentiable rendering. WebGPU is the API of the mini engine.

9. SteadySplats: Resampling of Low-Variance Gaussians for High-Fidelity Stochastic Rendering

Felix Windisch et al. (7 authors, with Chris Wyman, Georgios Kopanas, Bernhard Kerbl and Markus Steinberger) · preprint · first submitted 4 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It makes stochastic transparency practical for 3D Gaussian splats: Gaussians are rendered without sorting, and the result stays close to sorted 3DGS.
  • How it works. 3DGS normally sorts Gaussians by depth and alpha-blends them front to back. Stochastic transparency avoids the sort: each pixel keeps a Gaussian with a probability equal to its opacity and depth-tests it like an opaque surface. The expected result equals alpha blending, but at one sample per pixel it is very noisy. SteadySplats reduces the noise with history-based spatial resampling and temporal importance resampling, in the spirit of ReSTIR, and adds a training-time colour regularizer that lowers variance along each view ray.
  • What is new. Earlier stochastic 3DGS renderers were fast but too noisy to use. The authors report a 13 dB PSNR improvement at one sample per pixel over previous stochastic methods, in a Vulkan renderer.
  • Connection to CG. No sorting means splats can go through an ordinary depth-buffered engine pipeline and be mixed with meshes. See 3D Gaussian Splatting, ReSTIR in real-time ray tracing and splats in production engines in AI meets graphics engines.

10. Real-time Rendering of Pre-integrated Neural Emitters

Arno Coomans et al. (4 authors, with Markus Steinberger) · preprint · first submitted 5 Oct 2026

  • What it does. Neural Emission Fields (NEF) give noise-free direct lighting from geometrically complex light sources with a single network evaluation per shading point.
  • How it works. A network learns the illumination that the emitter produces in the volume around it. Its inputs are the shading point’s position, normal, view direction and material, and it has separate diffuse and glossy output heads. Training happens in the emitter’s local frame, so a trained NEF can be placed in other scenes under rigid transforms. Self-occlusion, interreflection inside the emitter, spatially varying emission and deformation are all baked in.
  • What is new. Analytic light models handle only simple shapes. Light sampling is noisy, and proxy methods still integrate radiance at run time. NEF moves the integral over the emitter’s surface out of the frame entirely.
  • Connection to CG. It pre-integrates the direct-lighting integral of the rendering equation, much as split-sum image-based lighting does for environment maps in real-time rendering techniques.

11. Masking Judder in Foveated Rendering with Phase-Shifted Noise

Ville Cantory et al. (4 authors, with Piotr Didyk) · preprint · first submitted 7 Oct 2026

  • What it does. When the periphery is rendered at a lower frame rate, as in temporally foveated rendering, motion there looks jerky (“judder”). This paper hides the judder with cheap synthesized noise.
  • How it works. Translating a Gabor kernel is the same as shifting its phase. So by modulating the phase of procedural Gabor noise over time, the method creates apparent smooth motion without re-rendering the noise. Given the on-screen angular velocity and the reduced temporal rate, it chooses a spatial-frequency band in which the noise masks the judder without adding visible aliasing of its own.
  • What is new. Earlier work used noise to restore spatial detail and the perception of speed lost to foveation. Temporal filtering suppresses judder but costs compute and blurs detail. The authors’ user experiments report a substantially wider range of speeds that look smooth.
  • Connection to CG. It is perception-driven rendering for VR: compare the foveated rendering demo in the Interactive Lab and embodied AI meets XR and HCI.

12. Neural Caching of Prefiltered Radiance for Specular Lighting

Dmitrii Klepikov and Vladimir Frolov · preprint · first submitted 8 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It is a variant of neural radiance caching (NRC) that also works for glossy and specular surfaces, in real time and adapting online.
  • How it works. NRC trains a small network online to predict outgoing radiance at path vertices, so paths can be cut short. This variant parameterizes the query by the reflection direction and trains a roughness-dependent target: it predicts prefiltered incoming radiance. That prediction is combined with a precomputed BRDF integration table through the split-sum approximation, the factorization real-time engines use for image-based lighting.
  • What is new. Classic NRC struggles with specular lighting, because outgoing radiance there changes sharply with the view direction. The authors report faster convergence to a path-traced reference and better specular quality on the Bunny and Specular Sponza scenes.
  • Connection to CG. It combines two standard tools: radiance caching from real-time ray tracing and the split-sum approximation from real-time rendering techniques, with the microfacet BRDF from physically based rendering.

13. A Hybrid and Hierarchical Ray Tracing Method for Efficient 3D Gaussian Rendering

Tiancheng Zhao et al. (6 authors) · preprint (cs.AR) · first submitted 9 Oct 2026

  • What it does. H2-Ray co-designs the algorithm and the hardware to speed up ray-traced 3D Gaussians on RT-core-style ray-tracing units.
  • How it works. It has three parts. LB-SBVH is a density-aware uniform-grid BVH that balances the work per node. RCPR lets one proxy ray share its traversal state with neighbouring rays. UIE is an intersection datapath that handles both Gaussian and triangle primitives, with 40% of its floating-point units shared.
  • What is new. Ray-traced Gaussian renderers such as RaySplats suffer from load imbalance, redundant traversal and mixed primitive types on current GPUs. Using a cycle-accurate model of a modified RT core plus CUDA timings on an RTX A5000, the authors report a geometric-mean speedup of 3.77x, and up to 9.26x, over RaySplats.
  • Connection to CG. Ray tracing Gaussians, rather than rasterizing them, gives secondary effects such as reflections, shadows and distorted cameras. See BVHs in ray and path tracing, hardware RT in real-time ray tracing and 3DGS frontiers.

14. Geometric Queries on Tessellation-Free Displaced Surfaces

Bing Xu et al. (3 authors) · preprint · first submitted 15 Oct 2026

  • What it does. It answers surface sampling, specular path search and closest-point queries directly on displacement-mapped surfaces, without first tessellating them into triangles.
  • How it works. The method builds a texture-space hierarchy. Each node stores a local affine height plane plus a conservative bound on how far the true height deviates from it. From the plane and the bound it derives distance and intersection bounds, area estimates for sampling, and slope bounds for specular path search, each with its own traversal algorithm.
  • What is new. Earlier tessellation-free methods mostly handled ray intersection and stored only min/max height bounds, which throw away how the height varies across a node. The first-order (planar) bounds are tighter and support many more queries.
  • Connection to CG. Displacement maps add fine detail without storing more geometry, a goal shared with virtualized geometry such as Nanite in inside production engines. The queries are the building blocks of geometry processing and of path tracing.

3. Neural rendering

NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, reconstruction, feed-forward 3D and relighting. Three SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 papers extend what a Gaussian scene can contain: X-ray interiors, discrete object states and volumetric video.
